If the Bill goes through this evening, as I believe it will, and when it receives approval from all sides of the House, as I believe it will, then the whole discussion of a separate line Department and the whole discussion of an official multiculturalism commissioner must be at the top of the priorities list when we try again to improve and to build upon this multiculturalism Bill.
I am saddened that we have not done it in this first window of opportunity. The possibility was there. It was particularly there among the members of the standing committee. It was there within the constituencies. It was there within the major organizations which tried to lobby the Government in terms of delivering the aspirations that they knew existed in their communities. There was a national consensus. I feel saddened that the Parliament of Canada, and in particular this Government, was not able to harness that consensus and pass those very important parts of the committee report.


Not only were the recommendations of the Opposition or various Members of Parliament ignored, but also the recommendations a number of major organizations. Most of them are voluntarily organizations whose members give up their time and energies to meet on Saturday afternoons, travel to Edmonton for their annual meeting, or come to Ottawa for consultations to meet with Members, Ministers, and bureaucrats. They too were not listened to.
I was somewhat amused when the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Weiner) stated that here was a Government that was prepared to listen and to act. That is not the case with respect to the recommendations, studies, and statistics that were drafted and presented to the Government.
One of those major organizations, the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, a number of whose representatives are in the gallery this evening and watching this debate on Bill C-93, in a major report dated April, 1988 made a number of very important recommendations and suggestions for amending Bill C-93. In its executive summary on page 1 it stated: "the Bill is currently a statement of wishes and ideals. The amendments we are suggesting will ensure that the Bill is meaningful and effective". The Council went on to provide three priority resolutions: the whole question of fundamental characteristics, which we were able to achieve today in a spirit of co-operation from all three sides; a clear commitment to implement the multiculturalism policy in Section 3.2, which was not delivered upon; and the monitoring of the implementation of the Act by an independent officer modelled along the same lines as the Official Languages Commissioner, which was not acted upon. Those are the three major recommendations.
The council also has a summary of recommendations from 1 through 14. How many of those recommendations found themselves into the finality of this Bill? The Council also listed other issues that it considered important in terms of crystallizing important concepts in principle in the Bill: the question of multiculturalism funding; the question of a separate Department; the question of the charitable tax status; and the question of the cabinet committee on multiculturalism, and a multicultural institute.
The Minister stated that he listened. He certainly did not listen very much to this report or to any other major report that tried to move the Government in recognizing that national consensus.
Then there are the committee hearings. First, the Government did not want to send Bill C-93 to the permanent Standing Committee on Multiculturalism. It preferred to send it to the legislative committee. In my humble and respectful submission, it received very shoddy treatment. From the first day of the meeting of the legislative committee it was very apparent to me that the priority of that legislative committee, dominated by Conservative Members of Parliament, was simply to get this Bill back into the House for report stage as quickly as possible and at any cost.
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Witnesses were not allowed to come before the legislative committee. Scores of witnesses wrote in stating that they would like to present recommendations. They were not allowed to appear. Many witnesses said: "If you are not going to allow us to appear, then have the committee travel and come to see us". That was also refused. In this first major multicultural legislation in four years witnesses from across the country were denied legitimate and justified opportunities to give their input and recommendations.
The committee was in such a hurry that it closed off debate and did not want to listen to any further witnesses. When my colleague, the New Democratic critic on multiculturalism, was not able to attend a drafting session of the amendments, the committee did not even have the respect to hold a meeting the next day in order that my hon. friend was able to attend. That is how quickly the Conservative Government wanted to get this Bill back into the House. The opposition amendments were moved in committee by government Members to attempt to defeat them in order that those amendments would not be able to see the light of day during report stage.
I do not think that that speaks highly of the motives and of the genuine interest in upgrading and amending and offering an input in partnership with constituents and organizations that enhance multiculturalism. They are the people in the trenches outside Parliament who translate the policies that we talk of into a crystallization of reality on the streets of this country. I say those things, not as a Member who is simply attempting to "cry the blues" but as a Member who is trying to have the public recognize that the process followed in this first multicultural legislation was very different from the course and the processes that have been followed in other pieces of legislation, which in some cases although important legislation were not as significant to the national fabric as this particular piece of legislation. In my opinion that process was not honoured to allow maximum participation of constituents to enhance and better a piece of legislation.
I am pleased that the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Charest) is present. I look forward to hearing his debate. I am sure that he is not familiar with the process that took place. If he has any questions he can rise.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. There is a rule in the House that has been long established and usually respected by Members of Parliament that when they address an issue or a piece of legislation they make their remarks pertinent to the piece of legislation.
I wish to point out that the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) has made so many long and vented complaints about the Government and partisan remarks that I do not think he is serving well the multicultural community that he pretends to serve. His real objective is to discredit the Government, and that has become very obvious. We can only regret the fact that he has made such a cheap issue out of a piece of legislation which he from time to time pointed out was the first of its kind. The Government and other Members from all sides


Canadian Multiculturalism Act
of the House merit some congratulations, but instead we get this type of rhetoric.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Minister may want to enter debate. That was not a point of order. The Hon. Member for York West.

Madam Speaker, I make no apologies to that Member or to any other Member for my actions and my commitment. I look forward to him rising on debate and respecting other Members. I look forward to his vision of the contributions of multiculturalism. I encourage him to rise as an individual and have the courage of his own convictions rather than take cheap shots and then return to signing his mail for his own Department, as much as that is important to do. 1 ask the Hon. Member to rise and discuss multiculturalism and to show the House his commitment, actions, and philosophies. If he wants to take shots at Members of this House, if that is his preference or obligation, I encourage him to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I do not wish to belabour the point, but the fact is that I think the same rule to which I referred a couple of minutes ago applies. The Hon. Member should keep his remarks relevant to the question before the House. I might add that we have a very competent and good Minister of multiculturalism whose remarks I fully adhere to.

Madam Speaker, I apologize. The Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport is quite correct. My comments were irrelevant when I referred to him. He pointed out that I should get back to relevancy, and I will do so.
The other aspect that I wanted to point out was that the proof of the discontent is not only lodged with members of the Opposition or Members on this side of the House. One only has to look at a number of witnesses and organizations that have commented on Bill C-93. I draw the sports Minister's attention to these individuals. Are these individuals wrong as well? Are these individuals and organizations also misguided?
We have individuals like Lome Waldman of the Jesuit Centre for Social Faith and Justice, who said: "I am in agreement with the position taken by the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism and am in particular in agreement about the need to create a Commissioner for Multiculturalism. I believe that the role of such a Commissioner ought to be clarified and strengthened".
Dr. Bhausaheb Ubale, Commissioner for the Canadian Human Rights Commission, said: "The proposed Multiculturalism Act changes nothing and it is not historic as the Minister calls it. It is purely symbolic. It is old wine in a new bottle."
Daniel Iannuzzi, President of Multilingual Television and editor of a weekly Toronto Italian newspaper, Corriere Canadese, said: "What we need is the recognition that
multiculturalism is an integral part of Canadian society-the Bill does not allow for such an interpretation."
The Ontario Advisory Council on Multiculturalism and Citizenship said: "The decision not to establish a Ministry as it was recommended by the standing committee is unacceptable and it only demonstrates the lack of leadership commitment for multiculturalism as a fundamental goal for Canada."
Michael Lanphier, for the Refugee Documentation Project of York University, said: "It is recommended that a new Department of Multiculturalism become the lead Ministry in negotiating an enhanced role for multiculturalism in every federal department".
The Ontario Council of Agencies Serving Immigrants said: "The establishment of a Commissioner of Multiculturalism along the lines of the Office of the Commissioner for Official Languages, could greatly assist in monitoring and encouraging the implementation of a multiculturalism policy."
The National Congress of Italian Canadians said: "We believe a Commissioner of Multiculturalism will bring the important elements of visibility and a greater accountability to the implementation of multiculturalism policies."
Lewis Chan, President of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council-and formally he made the statement when he was vice-president-said: "It is a shining symbol, and certainly a step forward, but it is a symbol without substance."
The Canadian Multilingual Press Federation said: "By implementing only one of the major recommendations of the committee report, the Government is offering Canadians virtually nothing new from the policies established in 1971."
The Canadian Hellenic Congress said: "David Crombie has rejected the idea of a new Department of Multiculturalism. The current treatment of multiculturalism policies within the Government of Canada is unfocused and underfunded. We doubt that the passing of the proposed Act in its present form will do much to focus or strengthen such policies."
The Hellenic-Canadian Federation of Ontario said: "We are profoundly disappointed by the Government's recent legislation on multiculturalism. We are displeased by this action of the federal Government, which undermines the work of the standing committee, and amounts to nothing more than window-dressing. Indeed, it simply reiterates what exists in federal practices. Unfortunately, there is nothing in the recent draft legislation on multiculturalism of substance for the people of this country."
Those are some of the comments, not of opposition Members but of organizations, of living and breathing entities in our constituencies and across our country that have a deep feeling, as deep a sense of feeling for this policy as any individual in this House. Those kinds of statements were also reflected by a number of the major medias. One has to read the headlines in major medias like The Ottawa Citizen, which call this Bill an empty promise on multiculturalism. It said, "This Bill will be a


disappointment to Canadians from all ethnocultural backgrounds. It fails to give teeth to the fight against prejudice and racism and, on the other hand, it makes an irresponsible promise on language that could rekindle old arguments. In sum, it is a mish-mash of circle squaring ambiguity and clumsy opportunism."
The Globe and Mail: "Multiculturalism bill gets cool welcome". The Montreal Gazette: "Multiculturalism bill ignores proposals by panels of MPs". The Vancouver Sun: "Ethnic bill called symbol over substance". The Vancouver Sun: "Ethnic bill gets mixed reviews". The Telegraph-Journal from New Brunswick: "Multiculturalism bill criticized". The Globe and Mail: "A multicultural mist". The Star-Phoenix from Saskatoon: "Multiculturalism legislation ignores major recommendations". The Chronicle-Herald from Nova Scotia: "New multiculturalism act short on means to implement programs". It goes on and on.
Again, these are not commentaries from members of the Government or on the opposition side; these are from individual organizations and media outlets across the country that have taken a look at this piece of legislation and have made a commentary.
I wanted to summarize some of my thoughts and try to crystallize in a few words what one has experienced over the last three and a half years in this administration leading up to this Bill. The concept of the multiculturalism Bill and the Canadian Multiculturalism Act was an important and significant one. I am saddened to witness that that window of opportunity was not utilized in a more profound way and in a more genuine fashion, in a way that there was a national consensus in the community and within Parliament.
I believe, notwithstanding those shortcomings, that it would be somewhat irresponsible for Members of this House or political Parties to try at the very least to deny the creation of a new Bill and of an Act. As I have stated-and it is very obvious-I would have preferred, as many other organizations, to be able to stand this evening and pass and approve a multiculturalism Bill that came a lot closer to reflecting the aspirations and desires of a country and of a collection of ethnocultural organizations from one coast to another.
I suppose that those ideas and visions that are not embodied and encompassed in today's Bill will become a reality that future Parliaments and a future Government may wish to have and hopefully will be successful in attaining.
I am pleased to have at least played a small part in the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism that tried to show the way for this Government to follow. I am also proud to say that it was a very co-operative committee including Members from all sides who I believe worked very well together. I also commend the members of the Government on the committee for having stayed the course and for having proposed and worked with members of the Opposition in providing a unanimous committee report that really showed the way which the Government should have embraced.
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Notwithstanding that, I am pleased to have participated on that committee. I recognize that there is much more work to be done in the area of this multiculturalism Bill. I suppose the constituencies and the member organizations will see this as a start, as a beginning that needs to be worked upon as the initial foundation to hopefully what will become a much more durable, encompassing and dignified Bill, an Act that reflects the aspirations and the work of Canadian citizens from all walks of life, from all backgrounds in Canada, right across the regions and territories.
Madam Speaker, perhaps Members will allow me to comment on how pleased we all are that I am restricted to 20 minutes-
Oh, oh!

-and will have to be concise. I know, Madam Speaker, that you wished I had unlimited time because I could use it well. I shall endeavour in a few minutes to consider the question that faces us on the third reading of Bill C-93 as the position we want to take.
Beginning more seriously with my observations, I feel honoured to speak at third reading debate on Bill C-93 on behalf of my colleagues and to consider the place that we should give to this Bill in the evolution of Canada's multicultural policy. We were very critical of the Bill at various points. That was true as we began consideration of the Bill at report stage.
Even though we have reached debate on third reading this evening immediately following report stage consideration, it is necessary to step back a bit and consider what we have been doing and what we have as the end result. We have to say that the Bill could do much more but, as everyone will concede, half a loaf is better than none. My friend, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) spoke of a window of opportunity. I am not very inclined to that kind of language. I think we could have seen another Government doing it much better. I would have liked to see a New Democratic Government providing the kind of multiculturalism Bill that would give structure and strength and put the policy in action, but we have not been given that opportunity by the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext: And you had such a good start to your speech.

We are in the seventeenth year of the multiculturalism policy. This is the first time we have had a Bill carried to this extent. Given the years in which the Liberal Governments did not produce and what the Conservative Government has chosen to put forward, we are considering it in that kind of context.
It would be appropriate to recognize the fact that we are a nation that requires a multiculturalism policy. Surely recognizing that it is in the seventeenth year of the policy that we are debating, we can look back and recognize that in 1971, when


Canadian Multiculturalism Act
the policy was announced in Parliament and accepted by all of the Parties represented at the time, there was a recognition of diversity of this country which made it necessary to move beyond the establishment of the policy of official bilingualism to provide for diversity that involved other elements.
As a matter of fact, in those years the people of Canada began to realize-we discovered last week that they still do not all realize it, by any means-that Canada could not exist simply as an English-speaking country and accepted a policy in which the federal Government would seek equality of French with English. Governments moved very quickly to recognize that it was not possible to see the country in bicultural terms. In those same years during which the policy of official bilingualism was established, the people of Canada began to recognize that there were fundamental realities, elements one might even say, in terms of the aboriginal peoples of this country who would go on and not be assimilated and who asserted their distinctiveness. We have been involved in these years since 1969 and 1971 in coming to grips with that.
We recognize that the policy of official bilingualism found expression in a Bill as early as 1969, and that a Commissioner of Official Languages was established to ensure that the policy of official bilingualism would be respected by federal institutions. It has never been easy work. Commissioners have often faced challenges in government and outside government in asserting that policy, but there was a commitment to it. I think one can relate those events of 1969 to 1971 and the succeeding years and the limited action that occurred on multiculturalism with events of the 1980s when, in the course of constitutional renewal following on the referendum in 1980 and the development of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, repatriation of the Constitution occurred. In the initial drafts there was not provision for the aboriginal peoples, nor any recognition of multiculturalism.
Those elements were added to the Charter. In Section 27 we have the important statement that the Charter shall be interpreted in such a way that it preserves and enhances Canada's multiculturalism heritage. At that point the Province of Quebec was left out of developments. Though the policy of official bilingualism was established in the Charter, there still remained work to be done.
Obviously I do not have time this evening to do anything like justice to what has occurred in the last year or two in this area, but there are many questions. I mention this as a way of suggesting a completing of the process in recognizing the linguistic duality of our country as a fundamental characteristic and making other provisions for the history of Quebec within Canadian society. That struck many people as inadequate. I mention it this evening because at report stage on a Bill that did not deal properly, so many people felt, with the fact of ethnocultural racial diversity in this country, we have succeeded by one means or another through the co-operation of the three Parties in having fundamental characteristics put into the Bill. That is a very important achievement, and one of the developments out of report stage that allows me to be less
critical of the Bill than I was when it was first tabled back in December, 1987.
It remains that though we have made various kinds of progress in recognizing diversity in our country, it was as late as 1987 that we had a Bill, and it is as late as 1988 that we are debating this particular Bill which still has the kinds of limitations that force one to speak of half a loaf and is reason to leave too many Canadians still feeling that the Government of Canada does not recognize diversity in anything like the way it should.
Perhaps I can consider the evolution of ideas about multiculturalism in this Parliament and relate those critically enough to the Bill again, because that too is appropriate at third reading debate. Suddenly in June, 1985 we had a standing committee struck. That was an important development however it occurred. I would like to have the inside story of that told to me sometime, but the standing committee was struck and got to work. It succeeded over the next two years in developing the agenda for multiculturalism policy in a report that was supported by all members of the committee and issued in June, 1987. The standing committee made recommendations on the means that we saw the Government of Canada requiring in order to take in all the Fine principles of 1971, all our perceptions of diversity in this country. There was a need to ensure that the Government of Canada respected that diversity.
As the Hon. Member for York West has already noted, among the most important suggestions is the proposal for a full-fledged Department of Multiculturalism with a Minister and a Deputy Minister. We have a proposal for a commissioner of multiculturalism who would ensure that this Department, all other Departments of Government, and all federal institutions would respect the policy first enunciated almost 17 years ago and only now being legislated. There were proposals for a genuinely representative advisory council, for a centre for multiculturalism.
These various proposals are the ones that I had in mind at the outset in saying that another Government might have seen-though the Liberals for years past had not and the Conservatives have declined to see it-the challenge and have acted on it in a full and significant way.
What happened in committee represented a refusal by the Government to act on the understanding that all the members of the standing committee had arrived at. After all, that committee, like all the other standing committees, was composed of seven members: five government members, one Liberal and one New Democrat. Private members in the government caucus had come to realize the necessity of these institutions.
When the report was released, it was distributed widely in Canada. I took the liberty, after some of the events including the refusal in the committee to face up to the experience of


racism in Canadian history, which left me in no doubt that we had to say these things and to press for firm action by the Government on multiculturalism, to issue my own minority report entitled "The Living Diversity: Multiculturalism for AH". It was designed to comment on the work of the committee and to press on the report.
These reports were circulated widely in Canada. Then the Standing Committee finally began its consultations to learn what persons in the various provinces and the great cities of our country thought about our recommendations, the extent to which they supported them. When we began that process in the City of Toronto, we found ourselves being upstaged by this Bill, Bill C-93, which the Government suddenly tabled. This Bill declined to take up the challenge in the way all the members of the standing committee thought it should.
At those first sessions in Toronto we found group after group supporting our report and critical of what the Government put forward. It was felt to be largely a symbol, as the now President of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, Lewis Chan, said so very well at the time. Many of those who appeared before us had these things to say.
The National Congress of Italian Canadians pointed to the subversion of the consultation process that was taking place and the fact that the Government had tabled a Bill which laid out a much more restricted and constrained statement of multiculturalism than the standing committee had wanted. There could be little doubt that the attempt to achieve a large statement of multicultural policy and to provide the machinery required to ensure that it is respected across all the institutions of the federal Government had failed.
In the work of the legislative committee there were similar shortcomings. There were suddenly constraints put on the number of witnesses we could hear in Ottawa. Suddenly we were rushed into consideration of amendments and that whole sorry process of defeating a large number of amendments in my absence and in the absence of the Liberal member of the committee took place. I will not make very much of that because report stage in the House today compensated for what went wrong in committee. That is why the process has taken the time it has in the House today. It is because the committee process was abused.
The reality is that this country cries out for action on a multiculturalism policy. The demographic realities of the country and the diversity of our great cities, a diversity that is being added to as Canada continues to respect its place as a country to which refugees, persons in danger of life and limb, can come, cry out for this multiculturalism policy. As immigration continues and as the great cities and regions of Canada become more and more diverse, society cries out for the policies to which we are supposedly giving our support in this Bill. Yet, there is so little in the way of assurance beyond what is given to us in language as weak as Clause 6, for example, which provides that Ministers of the Crown other than the Minister "shall", in the execution of their respective mandates,
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
take such measures as they consider appropriate to implement the multiculturalism policy of Canada. I suppose Ministers never take action that they consider inappropriate, but to have an invitation to find things inappropriate in the very language of a Bill leaves me gravely concerned about what we are doing.
This, of course, is the context within which one has finally to decide what to make of the Bill, what kind of position to take. I note that there has been a good deal of support, although sometimes I wonder about the support that there has been in the ethnocultural communities. Who can blame them? They have watched for years while the Liberals did nothing until they brought out that draft in 1984 which was so much weaker than this Bill. Nothing happened and then there were three years or more of this Government. One cannot blame anyone in the communities for thinking that they had better grab what they have now.
The Hon. Member for York West put a number of things in a critical light by quoting all kinds of persons. Of course, I put my critical observations on the record last December. The Canadian Ethnocultural Council was very critical of the Bill at the time, as the Hon. Member knows.
In nearing the conclusion of my comments, I think it is appropriate to note that the Canadian Ethnocultural Council put out a release on Tuesday of last week in which it announced its support for Bill C-93 and urged all three Parties to ensure early passage of it. The President, Mr. Lewis Chan, said:
Bill C-93 is much stronger today than when it was introduced seven months ago. It is a now in a form that we can support and in a form that we would want to see entrenched in law. The Government and opposition parties have listened to us and improvements have been made.
The release goes on to note three priority amendments. The first is a stronger commitment to implement multiculturalism, the priority involved in the change from "should" to "shall" in Clause 3. Second is the importance of having "fundamental characteristic" rather than "fundamental element" in the Bill. As I have already said, we finally achieved that this afternoon.
Third, there is the concern about an independent mechanism such as a commissioner to monitor the Act's implementation. The reality is that we failed in that area. We failed not so much because the Government was unwilling to spend the money, it seems. The Minister will have five officials in his Department involved in monitoring across the Government to ensure that Departments respect the policy. This is obviously an attempt to provide push from the Minister's quite junior position within the Department of the Secretary of State, and it is a long way removed from the kind of independence the Commissioner of Official Languages has.
We have quite simply failed to move the Government in these areas. We clearly have at best-a phrase I have used other places and it would only be fair to use it here-the first half of what could be quite a good Bill. As far as it goes, it is a pretty good piece of legislation and that is reason for supporting it.


Canadian Multiculturalism Act
My colleague talked about a window of opportunity. As I said before, I am not prepared to go so far as to use that phrase. The fact remains that a Government has chosen to bring forward a Bill which does at least this much in the way of legislating multiculturalism. For that reason, my colleagues and I intend to support the Bill and to vote for it.
We have no illusions about what we have actually accomplished. We still fear that we are far too close to symbolism rather than to real power in achieving multiculturalism. Few things could impress me as strongly in this area as the process in which we have been involved in the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism over the last months of trying to come to grips with what began when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) sent a letter to provincial premiers urging them to boycott events organized by three Canadian Sikh organizations. The committee has attempted to meet with the Minister to have him clarify what he is about. Tie continues to insist that it is entirely a matter of terrorism and has gone to another committee instead of coming to meet with us.
We have endeavoured to force the Minister and to press the Department to recognize that he is not dealing simply with Canadian Sikhs but with other communities: Armenian Canadians, Ukrainian Canadians, Baltic Canadians. I think the Department of External Affairs has failed the Canadian people and has refused to respect multiculturalism as a commitment of the Canadian Government. It has done that time after time. When the Minister refuses to appear, continues to show contempt for us, sends the Associate Undersecretary of State for External Affairs-actually, we demanded that he come-who is constrained by the strait-jacketing that such officials experience when they speak in public, then that is just one more piece of evidence of why we need much stronger legislation. It also illustrates why, although I will vote with my colleagues in supporting the Bill for what it does, the next Government will face the challenge of achieving what the ethnocultural communities of this country want.
I recognize the constraints on time and the fact that you have been generous with me for an extra minute or two, Madam Speaker. Thank you very much for the opportunity to say these things about the Bill. We are doing something that people will regard as historic. Given that, why should those efforts be as limited as they are so very often in this country? Why can Canadians not achieve the kind of greatness they want and have achieved in multicultural policy?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments? Debate.

Madam Speaker, I am sorry, but I did understand that according to the agreement we concluded earlier, everyone would get a chance to express his point of view on this Bill today. I know it is late. I
understand my colleagues' impatience. I will try not to impinge on their time, and I will even endeavour not to use up all of the time allotted to me. But still, as a parliamentarian, and I am probably among those who have served the longest here, I would like to make a few brief historical references to ensure that Canadian men and women who are listening to us, and Quebecers among them, understand fully that the process of building Canada is an ongoing, daily affair.
Before I make those remarks, however, I would like to very succinctly-and this is probably the specific reason which led me to ask for the floor-pay tribute to my colleague and friend the Member for York-West (Mr. Marchi) for the truly extraordinary work he has accomplished not only in the course of the past four years in Parliament but in all of the tasks which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) entrusted to him. He has discharged his duties in a remarkable way. His single-minded diligence could almost serve as an example for his colleagues, and I think he will not mind, nor will he take it as a form of misplaced paternalism if I pay tribute to him tonight and thank him on behalf of my party for the extraordinary effort he expended in his work.
As you know, Madam Speaker, and I will not attempt to be a historian tonight, this land of ours was at first Indian and Eskimo land, became a French and then a British colony, moved quietly toward partial autonomy and then obtained its independence and was governed by a great Prime Minister; all of our prime ministers were great in their own way.
He wanted to make his mark on the Canadian character of our institutions. We experienced ... I experienced the era of the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism. And so two languages and two cultures were to flourish in Canada, under Mr. Pearson.
Notice this development: two languages and two cultures. As though our first citizens simply did not exist! Make no mistake, we have a heavy responsibility to our first citizens. They may have been unhappy recently because they felt excluded from Meech Lake, and I will come back to that in a few minutes, but things must be seen in the context of the evolution of our country. Mr. Pearson felt, at that time, that there was a problem and called on eminent persons such as Jean-Louis Gagnon, Jean Marchand, Andre Laurendeau, Mr. Dunton, and several others to take a close look at this Canada that was evolving over the years and to attempt to define it.
Then there was the great Canadian flag debate, to make the flag authentically ours, which takes nothing away from the devotion some may feel for the flag of others.
Then there was the national anthem. I was directly involved as a member of the committee chosen by Mr. Pearson. It took 15 years until Canada's national anthem, which had been sung since 1880, was made official, as the committee recommended, in 1980.
Then came Mr. Trudeau, and I want to pay him tribute. In the early 1970s, he said, "Yes, bilingualism and


biculturalism!" But there is something new in Canada, a growing phenomenon that enriches us, namely the contribution of other communities. We therefore proclaimed that it would be better for this country, which we wanted to be bilingual and bicultural, to be known as bilingual and multicultural. It is a policy I believe in, one that I defend in French in Quebec. It is not easy and that is why I do so in French.

I just said in French that it is sometimes not easy to defend multiculturalism in the province of Quebec. I believe, and I repeat again, that if my name were "Prudomski" or "Prudomi-an" I would not understand why I should be less Canadian than those beautiful young Pages with us tonight who may be of English or French origin. We are all going to be equal and happy on an equal footing or we will not have a harmonious Canada.
How do we manage to have that harmonious Canada? It is true that the continuation of the Canadianization of our institutions has helped. After having proclaimed that Canada was bilingual and multicultural, we saw the repatriation of the Constitution and the creation of a Charter of Rights which is not yet complete. As long as you have in the Charter a clause saying "notwithstanding", we know it is not a complete charter. Any Government, federal or provincial, could use it, but hopefully not abuse it, until some day we amend that part of our Charter of Rights.
Then we have Meech Lake. That is not perfection on earth. Many people feel left out. However, it is a step toward a better Canada, a greater Canada, and a more Canadian country, more Canadianization of our institutions. It is going to be unique, so I am not going to quarrel with the Minister and the Government, saying that this piece of legislation could be better. It is not a finality, it is a step in the right direction.
I hope that Canadians will understand that the true meaning of the step which we have before us tonight is to remind Canadians to have the sensitivity to understand the feelings of others, to make them equal partners regardless of their colour or origin. If this piece of legislation helps, I will do as my colleague from the NDP and our able critic, the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), has done and vote for it. Even though we may have liked it to be different, it is a step in the right direction.
The French and English call themselves the two founding nations just as though the Indians and Eskimos did not exist. I find this expression a little bit arrogant. Max GrosLouis is a proud Indian leader in the City of Quebec from the Hurons. He always laughed when he heard me make big speeches about the two founding races. He looked at me from his height of almost six feet six, he clapped his hands and said, "Ha, ha, ha, where do I fit in this?" That really affected me. I realized that I lacked sensitivity to the Indians and I learned more about them, I learned to include them and to respect them.
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
What about those who came after the French and the English? They are so numerous now. We have an example in Toronto, everyone wants to be a candidate. I thank them because they want to take an equal part in the process. My colleague from Holland, who is not in our Party yet, is smiling. This is the new Canada that we are building together. There will be an election called soon, maybe this week, maybe next week, maybe next spring. There will be new candidates from new countries to which we are not accustomed in this House of Commons. We will have to adjust.
I hope they will be allowed to buy memberships.

I do not want to reduce this very important debate to the gutter. I will discuss that later. The Member may make comments on my speech after I am done.
I welcome ahead of time the new Canadians who are going to run for office. Who knows, I may not be here to do so when they arrive. I know they are going to help build a new Canada. They must feel equal regardless of their name, their country of origin, the colour of their skin, or the God to which they may like to pray, or even if they choose not to pray. That is the kind of Canada we must learn to build together.
If legislation such as the Bill we are about to vote on helps Canadians to reflect, that is good. It is permissible to dream. While I am speaking I am thinking of one of my passionate dreams, which is that maybe someday we will not need this kind of legislation, that there will be a day when Canadians have learned to respect each other so much that we will not need such legislation. We will understand that it is natural to allow Canadians to run for any office, to have the feeling that they are as important as anyone else, that they have as much chance as anyone to be nominated to any position. That is the feeling that we must develop together.
I know the Minister very well and he is not going to say that this legislation is imperfect, he will say that it is outstanding. However, I have learned to be more "conservative" as I have gotten older. This step will have to be ameliorated in the future by others.
Many amendments were put forward by the multicultural groups of Canada and were not accepted by the Government. Many amendments were put forward by my colleague, the Member for York West, and the critic from the third Party. Regardless of the fact that they were not accepted, we will vote for the Bill.
I hope that by attracting the attention of Canadians to such legislation we will also bring to their attention the importance of respecting people who are not of French or English origin. Those of French and English backgrounds have a responsibility, not only to respect the newcomers but to remember that when the French came here there were already people here. It is our duty also to respect them.


Canadian Multiculturalism Act

speechtext:
Point of order, Mr. Speaker. I would like to contest, if I may, the procedural acceptability of this motion being on the Order Paper under "Motions". The reason I do that is this.
Traditionally, the heading "Motions" has been reserved for concurrence requests in reports of standing committees which have been prepared by this House through the efforts of the standing committee, an independent body of this House. Members of standing committees, as the Chair will know, have the right to request that a concurrence motion be put on the Order Paper and then any member of the committee can move that concurrence motion in order to have a debate. I suggest that if motions of this nature are allowed to be put on the Order Paper under "Motions", we will have a complete subversion of the private Members' process.
If you look at the Order Paper under "Private Members' Motions", you will see other motions of instruction which a private Member puts in a draw and takes the chance that the motion will be drawn from a hat and thus go through the regular private Members' motions process. The House will know that process was developed by the parliamentary reform committee to ensure that private Members' motions and Bills had a decent opportunity of receiving full consideration by this House.
A private Member drafts a motion exactly as my hon. friend has drafted his, puts it in a hat and hopes that it is drawn out. When it is, it goes to the private Members' committee for deliberation as to whether or not it will get one hour's debate, such as the motion of the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) on the Order Paper today, which says:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider
designating as potential parkland all military lands located in urban areas and
presently used for military purposes, once their present use is discontinued.
There are other examples on the Order Paper.
I suggest we have a process for private Members' motions. You will note this motion is on the Order Paper in the name of an individual Member. It did not flow from a committee. It is an individual Member's effort to bring something to the attention of the House. It is a subversion, in my opinion, of the private Members' motion process and private Members' Bill process which was instigated and enacted by this House. For that reason I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friend is trying to do something by way of Motions which he should quite properly do by way of a private Members' motion.


Motions
Second, I suggest that the committees in this House are the masters of their own destiny. We set up committees under a legislative chairperson now, not under a government appointed chairperson. The Chair appoints those committee chairpersons from a panel and those committees operate and decide on the business of the committee independent of the House.
I think it is fair to suggest that the arrangement of the business of that committee, unless it is in the original motion sending the matter to the committee, should be left up to the committee. It is my understanding that, in this particular instance, the committee has decided not to travel.
It is very much the exception that committees travel. If one wishes to argue that this particular committee should travel, I would counter that by saying that standing committees of this House, one a joint committee with the Senate and one an independent committee of this House with no Senate membership, have already travelled this country to consider the issue of free trade. Before this legislative committee is the question as to whether or not Bill C-130 accurately brings into legislation the agreement between Canada and the United States on free trade. That is the narrow question before the legislative committee on Bill C-130. I think that speaks to why the committee should not travel.
In concluding my remarks I want to reiterate that I believe this motion should properly come under Private Members' Business, a motion for an allotted day, or proceedings on delegated legislation. Second, I want to refer to the argument which has always been before us, that is, that committees are masters of their own destiny. For those reasons I do not believe that this motion is in order.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT REQUEST FOR AUTHORIZATION FOR LEGISLATIVE COMMITTEE TO TRAVEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to reply to the Minister's point of order that this motion is out of order and should not be moved under Motions during Routine Proceedings.
I first want to refer to Beauchesne's Fifth Edition, citations 756 to 762 which list the rules and practices with regard to instructions to committees. I believe that if you consult these citations you will clearly find that the motion which the Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) has moved is in order in terms of the object which the motion seeks to achieve. Citation 756(1) states:
An Instruction is a motion empowering a committee to do something which
it would not otherwise do, or to direct it to do something which it might
otherwise not do...
Clearly, the object of this motion is to empower the committee to travel, a power which a legislative committee does not normally have, as the Hon. Minister has indicated. That is all the motion does. In that sense it is procedurally a "permissive" instruction.
Obviously, this type of motion has not been moved in this House by an opposition Member in a very long time. In fact, I believe the last time such an instruction was moved by
someone other than a government Minister was during the great pipeline debate in 1956. At page 604 of Journals for Wednesday, May 23, 1956, we find an instruction moved by Mr. Drew, seconded by Mr. Rowe, to enable the committee that was to study the pipeline legislation to divide the Bill into two separate orders.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, there was some discussion as to whether the motion required notice and whether or not the motion was debatable. Ultimately the Speaker of the day decided that the motion was in order and it was put to the House for a vote.
The principle which existed in 1956 has not been extinguished over time. The House now has the ability to instruct a committee to do something or permit it to do something that it might otherwise not be able to do. The right to move such instructions extends not only to government Ministers but to all Members of the House.
The right to move instructions is clearly recognized in Beauchesne. It is recognized in Bourinot at page 512 and in Erskine May Twentieth Edition at page 539. Nowhere in these citations does it indicate that such instructions can only be moved by Ministers of the Crown.
Proper notice has been given of this motion and it is my contention that the Hon. Member should be allowed to proceed with debate on this important issue. We are talking about enabling the committee to travel so that Canadians from coast to coast can come to these important deliberations and participate by presenting evidence on the effects of the trade deal. The Government may want to hide these hearings, to shut them off from the people of Canada, but we in this Party do not agree with this at all.
An instruction, if placed under Private Members' Business, as the Hon. Minister would have us do, would have almost no chance at all of ever coming up for debate. You, Mr. Speaker, know the process for private Members' initiatives. They go into a draw. I have had dozens in there for years which have never been drawn. In order to give instructions to a committee to act, we cannot go through the normal private Members' routine because the chance of that item being drawn for debate, and particularly for debate that would be followed by a vote, is virtually nil. It would be an exception.
If we are serious about giving instruction to a committee to travel this, in the absence of an initiative by a Minister, would seem to me to be the honourable way to do so, as has been tested time and again.
In response to the Minister's comment that there already had been travel, we all remember the farcical nature of the hearings when the committee was not debating the trade deal itself which was eventually signed by our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), but the issue of free trade with the United States. Hearings were held across the country, allowing one single day per province. I remember the day they came to the Province of British Columbia, which I have the honour of representing.


Hearings were held for a few hours and legions, if you like, of individuals and groups which wanted to have input into the process were turned away.
By the Prime Minister's own admission, this trade deal is the biggest trade deal signed, not in Canadian history, but in world history. If, as the Prime Minister has indicated, this is the biggest trade deal ever signed in world history, surely to goodness it would be appropriate to travel throughout the country this summer so that Canadians, wherever they live throughout Canada, would have an opportunity to participate in this discussion on the most important trade deal in world history.
We recognize the fact that in its present structure under the present rules and traditions the committee is unable to take the initiative to travel. That is why the Hon. Member for Essex- Windsor felt it was appropriate to move this motion so that the representatives of all the people of Canada in the House of Commons can give a clear instruction to the committee to do the honourable, decent, and correct thing, that is, to travel throughout Canada and hold hearings on what the Prime Minister himself describes as the most important trade deal in world history.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT REQUEST FOR AUTHORIZATION FOR LEGISLATIVE COMMITTEE TO TRAVEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we should start by looking at what a committee is supposed to be. A committee is clearly a subsidiary body to which a matter is sent for consideration by a larger body. The legislative committee which is studying Bill C-130 is clearly a subsidiary body of this House. In spite of the fact that the rules with respect to parliamentary reform may give a standing or legislative committee more authority to do things of their own accord, nothing in those rules has changed the fundamental concept of what a committee is.
A committee, especially the committee set up to study Bill C-130, is not a totally autonomous or independent body. It is nothing more than a subsidiary body of this House, to which this House has literally committed a piece of legislation for the kind of detailed study which was concluded some time ago and cannot be given in this Chamber as a House of Commons or even as Committee of the Whole.
I make this point because the Deputy Government House Leader seems to be arguing that somehow or other, under the rules reflecting parliamentary reform, our committees have such a status that once they are set up they are somehow cut loose from any link with this Chamber and it is somehow wrong for this Chamber to try to direct or instruct such committees.
If you consider what is the concept of a committee in principle and look at what our rules say, I invite you to conclude that the Deputy Government House Leader is wrong in inviting you to decide that under our rules it is no longer possible for this House to give an instruction to a committee as to how it should conduct itself. This House has no less
Motions
authority under our current rules than it did before the rules were adopted to give an instruction to a committee.
Incidentally, I find it ironic to say the least that the Deputy Government House Leader is basing his argument on the spirit of parliamentary reform when he and his colleagues on the Government side were so quick, so ready to throw parliamentary reform out the window when it served their purpose to do so in order to suspend the calendar concept under which we have been operating for some years so that the Government could get the House to sit through the summer.
Be that as it may, if the Deputy Government House Leader is interested in parliamentary reform and has returned to the view that parliamentary reform is important and should be supported, I maintain that there is nothing in our current rules under parliamentary reform which no longer makes it possible for this House to give an instruction to a group of Members who are nothing more than a subsidiary body of this Chamber.
It has already been brought to your attention that there are precedents that clearly set out what the authority of the House is to give an instruction to a committee. I want to draw your attention to some of the content of these precedents. You have already had drawn to your attention Citation 756(1) which says:
An Instruction is a motion empowering a committee to do something which it could not otherwise do, or to direct it to do something which it might otherwise not do. It directs the order and course of the committee's proceedings and extends or restricts the order of reference according to the discretion of the House.
We already know that this committee has shown itself through the efforts of the Conservative majority unwilling to seek the permission of the House to travel. I think we have clearly reached the point where it is appropriate for the House to adopt a motion giving an instruction to the committee studying Bill C-130 to travel from place to place, to hear directly the views of Canadians, where they live, where they work, where they make their homes, about the Government's trade deal with the United States.
It is clear from looking at Citation 759(1) that the motion which the Government has challenged could not have been called much earlier and that we are now at the appropriate point in time for such a motion to be made. Citation 759(1) states:
The time for moving an Instruction is immediately after the committal of the bill, or, subsequently, as an independent motion. The Instruction should not be given while the bill is still in the possession of the House, but rather after it has come into the possession of the committee.
We are just at that point contemplated by Citation 759(1). I suggest that the motion is very much in order from the point of view of the timing of its being called for debate.
I also submit that it is quite appropriate for this motion to be called under Motions rather than to be treated as a matter of Private Members' Business. I certainly can find nothing in the precedent set out in Beauchesne saying that this motion must be dealt with as Private Members' Business. I would say


Motions
that the whole concept of instructions to a committee by the House would be meaningless unless such instructions could be proposed as a motion during the point in time in our Routine Proceedings for the consideration of motions.
I repeat, there is no meaning whatsoever that could be attributed to the right of this House to give instruction to a committee unless it could be done in a way which would lead to a decision being taken on the request for instruction. This can happen only if it is done during the time set out in Routine Proceedings for motions.
I also suggest that it is consistent with the spirit of parliamentary reform to which the Deputy Government House Leader has once again become converted, after his unfortunate lapse in connection with cancelling our rules respecting the calendar concept.
If he is serious in regard to what parliamentary reform is supposed to mean, giving greater authority to individual Members to do things in the House, surely individual Members not of the Privy Council must be permitted to move motions to give instructions to committees during that item under Routine Proceedings entitled Motions. I believe the Deputy Government House Leader is very much in error when he argues that this motion can be presented only as a matter of Private Members' Business.
My friend, the New Democratic Party House Leader, says that a motion to instruct the committee with respect to such things as travel is rare and last happened during the pipeline debate. I have to take some issue with him on that because at page 230 of Beauchesne, paragraph 6 of Citation 761 states:
Power to adjourn from place to place-Instructions have been given to
committees to adjourn from place to place both within and outside Canada
for the purposes of receiving evidence. Journals, October 21,1976, p. 49.
There is a much more recent precedent on which to base our request that this motion be accepted and dealt with as quickly as possible. As recently as 1980, approximately, the special joint committee on the Constitution was authorized by this House and by the other place, I presume, to broadcast its proceedings after the committee was under way and without receiving any request from the committee that it be given such authority. That is a further precedent of this House giving instructions to a committee to do something it would not otherwise have the power to do. My hon. friend interjects to say that this motion to which I just referred was done on consent, but all consent means in this House is the equivalent of a unanimous decision of this House, but the consent does not always have to be given.
We are discussing whether this motion is in order, and I would like to say that rather than making the argument that this motion is somehow contrary to the spirit of parliamentary reform, if the Deputy Government House Leader and his colleagues have once again become converted to parliamentary reform, after their lapse with respect to suspending the
calendar in order to force the House to sit through the summer, they would welcome the initiative of the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) and the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), our critic on trade, who proposed motions to allow the committee to travel.
I want to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that I believe this motion is in order not only insofar as it intends to give an instruction to a parliamentary committee, but with respect to it being called during Routine Proceedings under the heading of Motions, and also with respect to the substance of the matter.
I think something that is very consistent with the spirit of parliamentary reform is to make it easy for Canadians to have access to their parliamentary institutions. One of the best and most effective ways to do this is through enabling committees to travel when they are considering something as important as this trade deal so they can get the views of Canadians where they work, where they live, where they have their homes, and where they will be affected by measures such as this Government's trade deal with the United States.
It is not satisfactory to say that a committee has already travelled for this purpose. As has already been pointed out, the travel of a previous committee was clearly inadequate with only one day in each provincial capital. In any event, the committee in question did not study the matter that is currently before the legislative committee on Bill C-130. It did not study Bill C-130, nor the trade deal itself.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to move to seek leave to adjourn the House for the purpose of discussing what I consider to be an extremely vital and pressing issue facing our country. That is the issue of water diversion from Lake Michigan, which could have devastating effects across the Great Lakes system and which would demonstrate to Canadians yet again how important water is within our relationship with the United States and how important it is that there be protection provided for us as a country to safeguard that water in the future.
Because we have such an important issue here, with many indications from the United States of pressure building in order for this diversion to take place, I hope that you will give very careful consideration to this request. Perhaps it might make sense to reserve judgment on it because of the importance of the issue to my constituency, to the many people across Ontario and to all people across Canada, and in view of the widespread implications of a diversion of this kind toward our relationship with respect to water with the United States in the future.
