speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).

Madam Speaker, I rise to support the amendment proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp), and to welcome the support for at least one of the amendments that he has proposed by the Government.
No Member of Parliament who represents any city in Canada can help but be aware of the tremendous changes which have taken place in terms of the people living in the cities of Canada in recent years. The constituency which I represent has always been recognized as an ethnic constituency, a constituency populated almost completely by immigrants; first, of course, by the immigrants who came from Great Britain and, later, by immigrants from Germany, Russia, Poland and many of the eastern European countries.
In the last 10 or 12 years we have seen a tremendous change in my constituency, as in many others, because beside the groups which I referred to earlier we now see people from Portugal, Italy, the Philippines, all the Caribbean countries, Central America, Africa, and Asia. From Asia we see people from India, Sikhs, Vietnamese, Chinese people from Hong Kong and from mainland China, Laotians and I am sure there are others who I have missed.
We also see a tremendous movement into the City of Winnipeg by native Canadians, who are moving to Winnipeg as they are to a number of other cities, from the reserves which they find completely inadequate to provide them with a decent standard of living.
A situation has developed in the City of Toronto where a majority of the students attending the public schools are neither from Anglo-Saxon nor French origin. This type of movement has created tremendous problems for the cities and for the people who come to this country. The issue of multicul-turalism was first raised by one of the members of the Bilingualism and Bicultural Commission appointed by the then Liberal Government, headed by Mr. Pearson. A resident of Winnipeg, Professor Rudnyckyj, who, while accepting the main recommendations and findings made by the commission, which dealt with the relationships between the French and the English-speaking people of this country, pointed out that an
increasing number-now a third of the population of this country-come from countries which are neither Englishspeaking nor French-speaking.
Many of these people come from countries which do not have, or ever had our democratic institution, our democratic way of life, our trade unions or co-operatives or civil liberties organizations. Many of them come here without the ability to speak either English or French. While canvassing in the older parts of my constituency I still come across women in their sixties or seventies who still cannot speak more than a few words of English.
In this country until a few years ago we did very little to deal with this problem. We are happy and proud to see the people who have come to this country. We are happy and proud to see the progress that they have made, but they need a great deal of assistance in making that transition from the country from in which they came in making that transition to this country which is so different.
It is not enough simply to give them the opportunity to work. Many of them work in some of the hardest, poorest paid jobs available in this country. We have to give them the opportunity to learn the language. We have to give them the opportunity to fit into our society. For many of them, Madam Speaker, the way in which they do that is based around and with the people from the same countries from which they came. Many belong to the hundreds of thousands of voluntary organizations which these groups have formed.
The Government of Canada and the Parliament of Canada in the early 1970s recognized the importance of helping these new ethnic groups to adjust and integrate into this country. We adopted in principle the idea of fostering the multicultural fact in this country. We have established a part-time Minister and part-time Department. It sounds good. It looks good when one reads about it, but the reality is we really have done very little.
If we compare, for example, the resources allocated for multicultural activities in my province-I will use my province as an example in which as I have indicated a very substantial percentage of the population comes neither from the Anglo-Saxon nor the French background of Canada-we find that what is allocated to help foster the various ethnic communities in the Province in multicultural activities is a very small amount compared to the money, the services and the assistance given to the Franco-Manitobans who make up a very small percentage of the population of Manitoba.
I am not for a moment questioning the assistance given to the French-speaking people of Manitoba. I, like most Members of Parliament regardless of Party, recognize the necessity and the justness of helping the French-speaking people of Manitoba and of every other part of Canada to foster, maintain and strengthen their language and culture. But when I compare the assistance given to them to the assistance given


for multicultural activities, I have to face up to the fact that what we are getting most is mere words.
I know that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon has put a great deal of effort into his work in this area. I want to say on behalf of myself and all members of the New Democratic Party that we support those efforts and we call on the Government, as we called on the former Liberal Government, to do more than say the right things, to do more than make pretty speeches, to do more than appearing at functions organized by various ethnic communities in this country. We call on this Government to take seriously the principles supported almost unanimously in this Parliament by all Members from all Parties to support the efforts of the new ethnic communities and of the native communities to help them maintain the cultures which they brought, all of which in the years to come will help to make this country a much better place in which to live.

Madam Speaker, I take great pleasure rising in today's consideration of Bill C-93, the Canadian multiculturalism Bill and to urge Members on both sides of this House to support this basic and fundamental amendment No. 6 to the Bill.
Some weeks ago the Minister of State responsible for Multiculturalism (Mr. Weiner) appeared before the legislative committee examining Bill C-93 and told the committee that he was willing to work with it to improve Bill C-93, as he stated in the House today. That is exactly what happened. The Bill which we are considering today is considerably stronger. It is considerably more vital than that with which we started in late March.
There have been amendments made to this Bill which strengthened it from the preamble to the very last clause. But one or two things have been left to be done here today.
The amendment which I proposed today makes this recognition even more clearly. Many witnesses appeared before the committee expressing their concerns that the multicultural nature of this society could be lost in other considerations and that the Bill was not sufficiently precise in underlining this fundamental characteristic of Canadian society. Many witnesses urged the committee to make a clearer expression of this matter.
The motion that I propose does so. This motion states simply and cleanly that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of our Canadian heritage and identity. In a few moments I will also propose an amendment which brings these clear, simple and precise words to the important preamble of the Canadian multiculturalism Bill.
Why have I chosen to make this motion? Why do I feel the words "fundamental element" are not clear enough? It is true that the Bill, even from its first reading, was clear in stating that multiculturalism was part and parcel of our identity and our heritage. But I feel that it is important to underline this. It is not only part and parcel, it is one of the foundations of our
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
identity and heritage. It is one of the foundations of Canada. That is why we adopted simple and precise language, language which has clearly entered our constitutional lexicon to express what multiculturalism means to this society.
I know my hon. friends, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) and the Hon. Member from Thunder Bay have proposed relatively similar amendments and I congratulate them for doing that. I do not think these particular amendments are well founded for a number of simple reasons.
The Hon. Members from York West and Thunder Bay have translated in their motions "fundamental characteristic" to be trait fondamental. If we are to use the same strength of language that is used in other places, we must use the expression caracteristique fondamentale. This is not just a matter of terminology. It is important that the language of this Bill in both official languages be crystal clear. I hope the House appreciates the motion that I am presenting today and I urge hon. colleagues from both sides of the aisle to support this simple motion, a motion which in both official languages underlines that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of our society.
I would like to take a few moments of the time of the House today to explain Motion No. 32 which clarifies and strengthens the preamble of the Canadian multiculturalism Bill.
Earlier in this debate I rose and urged the House to support a simple, clear and precise amendment to the multiculturalism policy of Canada which stressed that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of our identity and heritage. I would urge this House to accept a similar, simple and clear amendment to the preamble of the Canadian multiculturalism Bill which states in only a few words that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic in the continuing evolution of our nation.
This is an important amendment. The amendment shows that the Government has listened to those who appeared before the legislative committee examining Bill C-93. This simple amendment shows that the Government has been willing to work with the committee and with Members of this House to strengthen the Canadian multiculturalism Bill.
At this time there are two other amendments relative to the preamble, one presented by the Hon. Member for York West and one presented by the Hon. Member from Thunder Bay. These amendments are excellent in spirit, but they are flawed, I believe, in their creation. First, both amendments in the French language utilize the words "trait fondamental" as opposed to "caracteristique fondamentale". This is an important difference. It is an important shortcoming in both motions about which I spoke earlier today. If we are to signal what this amendment is about and to say that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic, and if we wish to give the language sufficient force, we must use the language which is already in the lexicon; namely, caracteristique fondamentale.


Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Second, both amendments presented by the Hon. Member for York West and the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay- Nipigon (Mr. Epp) muddy the waters. In the instance of the amendment of the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon, it mixes policy statements with preambular language. Policy commitments properly belong in Clause 3 of the Bill. A preamble sets the stage. It presents values. It is for that reason that I find the Hon. Member's amendment appealing but unsatisfactory.
In the instance of the amendment presented by my colleague, the Hon. Member for York West, I found repetition of words and ideas in places, and of course, the problem with its French translation and the weakness of that French translation. I think is important that we maintain simple amendments and that we put forward amendments in clear and precise language. It is important that we utilize the lexicon involved in this nation. For this reason, I would urge Members on both sides of the House to support the motion I have brought forward today and thus to recognize that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of our Canadian society.

Madam Speaker, I would like to join with my colleagues in saying a few words in this debate, particularly to acknowledge the very great importance of changing the language of the Bill through these amendments in order to strengthen it. Many groups across Canada have criticized this Bill because it appeared to be too soft and was in effect tokenism. These groups will certainly be pleased with this amendment, although at this stage we are only dealing with words. We certainly must toughen up other clauses of the Bill as well.
As I understand it, the change of wording in this clause will establish an equal partnership between all cultural groups within Canada. It will mean that people of both French and English origin will be recognized as being part of the fundamental characteristic of Canada and so too will be those from so many other countries. These in fact are the people who are now becoming the majority, certainly in western Canada. These people have origins other than French or English.
It is very important that this Bill not simply be a recognition of songs and dances, arts and culture, which is what some people think is meant by multiculturalism. It is absolutely essential that it have the strength to fulfil the spirit of the Charter. This means that there has to be equal opportunities and there has to be a removal of discrimination and racism that affects people from origins other than French or English.
In western Canada and particularly in the ridings of Vancouver East and Vancouver-Kingsway, by far the majority of new Canadians as well as second and third-generation Canadians are those who have come from Asian countries and those who are not Caucasian but are people of colour or visible minorities. It is absolutely essential that our multicultural policy begin to recognize that not all people of different cultures came from Europe. There is a very different stream of people who are coming from Asia, and in some cases the cultures are very different indeed. For those who come from China or some of the oriental countries, English must be learned in a much different way.


It is also very important to recognize that there is not a representation of visible minorities in the House, and that is very typical of the decision-making process across Canada. It is important that we take this matter seriously and that we strengthen this Bill so that it helps to facilitate and implement multicultural policies.
In the past few weeks, I have attended high school graduations throughout my riding of Vancouver East. I would say that only 5 per cent to 10 per cent of the students graduating from secondary schools are from Anglo origins and probably none are from Franco origins. The majority are young people who are members of visible minorities and have wonderful motivations to complete their educations. They will probably face barriers that are much greater than some of their colleagues at university.
It is important that the Bill not be seen as tokenism and that we recognize the real issues of racism and discrimination in Canada. The Government must do this by acknowledging the injustices of the past. I am referring particularly to the injustices to Canadians of Japanese origin who faced such terrible discrimination under the War Measures Act. People of Chinese origin were also discriminated against and had to pay a head tax and face the Exclusion Act, which was a purely racist Act.
It is time we acknowledged these injustices and provided fair redress so that our young people can grow up and be proud to say that regardless of their origin, regardless of the colour of their skin, they have equal rights in Canada.

Madam
Speaker, I wanted to say a few words following the Hon. Member's speech.
I can speak pretty openly here, I am losing my riding of Vancouver-Kingsway, and there are a couple of things 1 would like to say that I think Members might be interested in.
My riding has more Chinese Canadians than any other riding in Canada.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) said her's does.

There is some disagreement about that, but I think mine really does. As I said, the riding will be gone under redistribution in a couple of days, although I still remain the Member until the next election, but it has become a unique spot with respect to Asian immigrants. This is the new reality in Canada. It is a great plus for Canada. The way Canadians should look at the flow of Asian immigrants is to see it first as part of the continuous flow which builds the population of Canada. My parents came from Scotland when I was a young boy. The same thing is true for people from Italy and other parts of Europe. Now we have a wave of Asian immigration.
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
We should think of it as an advantage. This is where the advantage is.
Second, we are trying to reach out to the Pacific Rim. It is the fastest growing trading area in the world. Canada is on the edge of the Pacific, it is one of our oceans. We have this great resource of Pacific cultures in Canada. We have people who are bicultural. These sons and daughters of immigrants would become Canadians through our schools. We are different from the U.S. because of our multicultural heritage. It is inscribed in our Constitution. We have committed ourselves to saying to people that they can keep some of their heritage. We have great strength in that. The strength lies in these Asian Canadians. That will be in many ways a great help in getting Canada into the Pacific Rim, the Asian Pacific. We should be thinking about things in this way. It took me a while to think that way even in my own riding.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), an eloquent spokesperson for immigrants and multicultural groups and so on, raised the issue of past injustices. She talked about the Exclusion Act and the Chinese head tax and how she fought for compensation for those who were discriminated against.
Other people, including my predecessors from Vancouver- Kingsway, Grace Mclnnis and Angus Mclnnis, fought for redress for Japanese Canadians for the racist treatment they got in Canada during the war. I do not want to go into this in a lot of detail but I want to answer a question which I think a lot of Canadians do not understand. That question is: why deal with past injustices? I remember asking Pierre Trudeau in the House about compensation. He shrugged and said: "Why fight battles of the past?" The reason you have to deal with past injustices is to make sure they do not happen in future. We had the incident of a boatload of Jewish people who were turned away just before the war. Think about that. Think about what we did.
This is a great country, a just country. In spite of our shenanigans in Question Period and our debates and arguments in this House, look at the question I put today to the Minister of Communications (Mrs. McDougall). I asked her if she would take up the case of a fellow who had lost his son in this oil rig disaster and perhaps provide some legal representation. It is going a long way, but she took it up and said they would consider it. That is the best of Canada. We are an open and fair country. We have to make sure that that happens with our immigrants and the multicultural base of our country.
We passed a multicultural constitution in 1982. You know I have had troubles with the new one in 1986, but the one in 1982 was a magnificent constitution. Canada is like a cake, if I might say so. We have the native people at the foundation. Then the French and English. In the constitution we had the recognition of education rights, which I think is really important. Then on top was the recognition of the multicultural reality of Canada. That is a good vision of Canada.


Canadian Multiculturalism Act
We cannot just sit back and say we have done this kind of thing in law and symbolically. We have to do real things to help multiculturalism. I will give you an example. I do not know what other cities are like, but in Vancouver, English as a second language is the language of the majority of kids in the public schools. That is a difficult situation. It is difficult for the educational system. It may mean that the federal Government, dare I say it, may have some role in additional funding for English as a second language.
It is done now.

I know it is done now. I do not think the Government has much of a role right now because education is of course a provincial responsibility. However, we may have to look at it and say the federal Government has to help. If you are bringing in waves of new immigrants you have to help educate them in the English language. Parents want their kids educated in English or French in Quebec so that they get into the mainstream of Canadian society. We have to take the measures necessary to help multicultural groups retain their own language as well. We have the Ukrainian dancing groups, theatre groups, culture groups, that we support. We take a different view from the Americans. We do not take the melting pot view, we take a broader view where you can maintain some of your multicultural heritage.
I will sit down now. The Hon. Member for Vancouver East provoked me to speak because she gave such a good speech. I just want to come back to that one point which I would like Canadians to think about. I know it is sometimes very difficult, and I hear it in my community offices, "Why are you bringing all these immigrants in? They are different than we are." You have to look at the advantages of immigration. I think one of the big advantages is, especially with Asian Canadians, that instead of sending the traditional businessman to China to try to get a contract, we can send a Chinese Canadian whose family is there. He might be able to speak the language, has taken courses and brushed up on Cantonese or Mandarin at the Chinese Cultural Centre in Vancouver. That is a forwardlooking Canada and that is the way we should look at multiculturalism and immigration.

Madam Speaker, I would like to add my support to this Bill and congratulate the Minister on bringing it in. In my view a multicultural Bill has been long overdue in Canada.
I was raised in a cosmopolitan area, probably as cosmopolitan as any in Canada, namely the Drumheller Valley. During my lifetime that area has seen 21 or 25 coal mines, all of which have now disappeared. However, people came from practically every country of the world to work in those coal mines. The wonderful thing about the Drumheller Valley was that these people did not continue to call themselves Ukrainians or Hungarians or Britons, they called themselves Canadians. At the same time they retained their own language, their own customs. I want to pay tribute to those people today.
I want to deal with some specific people, the Ukrainians, for instance. Hundreds of them came to our coal mines. Hundreds of them came in their sheepskin coats and braved the blizzards, the chinook winds, and the droughts. They worked toward a better country. They tried to build a heritage.
Many people do not realize that the Ukrainian people were the first to work on the building of our railways across western Canada. They were later replaced by a large number of Chinese people. The Chinese people were certainly taken advantage of but they remained here. Many of them brought their relatives here and they have become excellent citizens.
Another large group in my area is the Italian community. As a matter of fact, the Italian community is probably the second largest in the Province of Alberta. The Italian group was notorious for bringing their language and customs with them. They still speak Italian in their homes today, but they speak English outside. They endeavour to keep the customs of their homeland.
Another large section is the German community. One of the first things I remember as a young boy during and just after World War I was the antagonism toward those of German descent. I remember my mother saying many times that none of us had any choice as to our nationality, colour, or creed; that it was the way we lived that really mattered. German people suffered a lot of persecution in Canada at that time, but they remained and are wonderful citizens. In my riding in Beiseker and Carbon there are some of the finest farmers in the world. They are doing their utmost to build a great Canada.
In addition to Ukrainian halls in the Drumheller Valley we had a Hungarian Hall. Many people came from Hungary and worked in our coal mines. Some of their descendants now hold high positions throughout Canada. A notable one is the head of the regional office of Parks Canada in Calgary. He came from a wonderful Hungarian family in the Drumheller Valley.
We have the Poles, the Americans, and the Dutch. The Dutch people have made a tremendous contribution too. They are not mentioned often. I attended the golden wedding celebration of a Dutch couple only a few weeks ago. They are symbolic of hundreds of others who have contributed to Canada.
The Spanish, Norwegian, Swedish and Danish groups have also made a wonderful contribution. A chap who originated from Sweden came up from the Dakotas into the Drumheller Valley. He was the first to drive oxen into Canada. There are histories of him throughout the Valley today.
I remember a young Japanese lad who lived in the old Midland Mine. His father was one of the finest citizens I have ever known. He loved Canada and loved our way of life. One of his boys served in the Armed Forces during the war.


We have the Jewish people and the Arabs. They may be fighting each other today, but not in the Drumheller Valley. They are Canadians. They brought their customs and their language, but they are now Canadians. We have the Koreans, the Vietnamese, and many people from that part of the world who are part of our population.
We talk about the English and the French, and they are the founding nations, but these others have played a tremendous part in building this country too. The Scottish, the Irish, and the Welsh object to being referred to as English people. They have their own customs and their own language.
We have people from Yugoslavia, India, Egypt, South and Central America, and Africa. People from all the continents have come to Canada, and I like to think of Canada as a multicultural country, not only as a two-nation country but as a great multicultural nation called Canada. I like to think of Canada as being a tremendous mosaic.
An honour I will never forget is when I was asked to represent Canada at the opening of the Pan-American Highway about 1965. The people in Mexico put on a tremendous outdoor show for the delegation made up of one American, two Canadians and people from Central America and South America under the auspices of the U.S. organization. At the show I saw dances of Scotland, Ireland, and the Ukraine. I saw aspects of almost every country which is now represented in Mexico. What a tremendous job an artistic director would have in Canada today to put on an outdoor show to exhibit the customs of all the nations which have become part of Canada. Someday I hope there will be a tremendous mosaic which will show what all these people have contributed toward building this great nation.
After all is said and done I like to think of the people of Canada, not as the English, the French, Egyptians, Hungarians, Germans, Italians, or Dutch, but as Canadians, because Canada is their country of adoption. They have made Canada their country and this has made Canada a greater and a better country.

Madam Speaker, in our continuing consideration of amendments to Bill C-93, this particular group includes some small changes in total bulk but represent very significant attempts to strengthen the Bill.
If it is in order, I would like to recognize the presence in the gallery of the President of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council and the past President. Of course, it is not in order, so I note that, in considering the motions before us here seriatim, Motions Nos. 10 and 11 are provided for in part by changes that were made in the legislative committee. My Motion No. 11 is designed to ensure that Clause 3(2) would read: "It is further declared to be the policy of the Government of Canada that all institutions shall-"
The Bill as reported from the legislative committee was amended to read "shall" rather than "should".
Having mentioned the Canadian Ethnocultural Council a moment ago, may I say that this is one of those very important points that this national organization of ethnocultural communities emphasized was necessary. The Bill initially was encouraging, but an absolute commitment was required by the Government of Canada to take strong action. That was


accomplished with the use of the word "shall" as it was changed in the legislative committee.
Unfortunately, it might still not be quite sufficient. Therefore, Motion No. 10 is designed to go beyond that. Motion No. 10 in the name of my colleague, the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), was accepted by the Speaker rather than my own. It is a motion which states that: "institutions shall, with a view to implementing the policy stated in Clause 3(1)." It places an even greater obligation on the Government of Canada to be sure that the policies to which Parliament is committing the Government and to which the Government itself is committed will be acted upon in the way of various specific proposals.
Motion No. 12 is my proposal for an explicit addition to the Bill designed to put into these obligations that the Government of Canada would accept, an obligation to act upon the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, specifically Section 27. This particular motion would commit the Government of Canada to develop policies and programs that assist ethnocultural communities to make larger contributions to the preservation and enhancement of Canada's multicultural heritage.
I would like to comment on the carrying of Motion No. 30 rather than Motion No. 32, proposed by the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Witer) and moved, by agreement, by the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Oostrom). Motion No. 30, moved by myself which was chosen over Motion No. 32, put into the preamble the language of Section 27 of the Charter in a way analogous to what was done in our consideration of the Official Languages Bill, Bill C-72, which was passed last week.
I think putting the language of the Charter into legislation is a useful exercise, so in Motion No. 12 I have endeavoured to commit the Government of Canada at the outset to acting on Section 27 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Motion No. 14 is designed to remove the word "promote" from several of the paragraphs in Clause 3(2) and insert instead the word "implement". Here again is a proposal that has come not only from the Canadian Enthocultural Council but from the various community organizations. If the Parliament of Canada is really serious about the multicultural policy we first adopted in 1971, we should have an actual obligation on Ministers and all Departments to implement the policy and to look for ways in which the policy could be made more real.
Motion No. 17, moved by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), is an alternative to the proposal in Motion No. 8. I endeavoured to take up the concern of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council to recognize explicitly in the Bill the importance of the youth of our country and to ensure that our multicultural policy was carried through with explicit regard to the youth of the country and their needs. One way to do that is to make it one of the principles on which the Government would be committed to act in the first section of Clause 3,
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
which is where my Motion No. 8 stands. The other way to do that, of course, is to use Motion No. 17, putting it in as one of the obligations of the Government.
I would hope that recognizing the Government rejected my Motion No. 8, although it was initially on a voice vote, the House might have the will to take up Motion No. 17 and make it an obligation. It is, after all, a strong request from the young people who are active in the Canadian Ethnocultural Council to have their needs recognized. I look to the Minister and hope there might be some readiness to take up this particular proposal.
There remains then, only one other motion on which I would like to comment. Motion No. 19 was found to be out of order because it went beyond the scope of the Bill as the Government presented it. I want to note that the motion moved by the Hon. Member for York West takes up the first paragraph of my motion. I take it, then, given the ruling on Motion No. 18, that Motion No. 19 would have been found in order if it had only gone that far, although it would have been an exact duplicate. I endeavoured to go beyond annual plans to provide for review on all those activities oriented to the establishment of a commissioner of multiculturalism which, again, the Government has not taken up.
Motion No. 18 has a very useful proposal that the Departments of Government have an obligation to make plans annually in order to realize the multicultural policy of the country. In the context of my motion being ruled out of order, but Motion No. 18 being in order, I speak in support of that motion as well as in support of the motions on which I have already commented.
These are important motions to strengthen the Bill. Let me leave it at that and look to the comments of others. I trust we will have the support of the House for these motions to ensure that this historic Bill really becomes the kind of legislation it should be.

Madam Speaker, I would like to address my remarks in the time allotted to Motions Nos. 10, 15, 17 and 18. Motion No. 10 which stands in my name is an attempt to make the language and commitment somewhat more specific. We have tried to move this intent at committee and today at report stage because I believe that if there is one ill with the Bill, it is its lack of commitment in terms of very specific, clear and committed language.
With respect to Motion No. 10, what I am endeavouring to do is to tie subsection (2) under the federal institutions to the earlier stated multiculturalism policy for the federal Government. The intention of Motion No. 10 is simply to review and to try to commit the federal Departments in a very specific way to the multiculturalism policy as articulated in subsection (1). Those words tying the federal departmental role to the federal policy is not stated explicitly. Rather than keep it vague and general in terms of having federal Departments expand and enhance multiculturalism, I would like to see the


Canadian Multiculturalism Act
role for the federal Departments tied to the very clear multiculturalism policy as articulated under subsection (1).
Motion No. 15 attempts again to expand on the principle and general scope of that particular clause on page 4, line 40. As it reads now, one of the roles of the federal institutions is to "promote policies, programs and practices that enhance the ability of individuals and communities of all origins to contribute to continuing evolution of Canada". I would also add the words "and that removed discriminatory barriers to their full and equal participation in Canadian society". This is an attempt to try to eradicate the specific problem that many Canadians all to often face in terms of discrimination in the workplace, in terms of vertical mobility and in terms of hiring practices.
The intent, as it now stands, generally addresses that concept. What 1 would like to do, and what many organizations would like us to do as a Parliament, is to make specific reference to the type of systematic barrier problems that Canadians face. Therefore, the intention of Motion No. 15 is to tie down explicitly the concept and make it very practical and specific, ensuring that one of our goals as a Parliament and as a Government is not only to talk about equality of opportunity but to do something about it and to come closer to ensuring that political, social and economical equality in our House and in our Constitution is predicated upon.
With respect to Motion No. 17, what I would like to replace is a reference under our federal institutions and our federal Departments, as the Canadian Ethnocultural Council's youth wing had advocated before the Standing Committee of Multiculturalism and before the legislative committee studying Bill C-93, to a specific reference and commitment to enhancing the policies, goals and objectives of multiculturalism specifically and target them to the youth of Canada. I think it is incumbent upon a Parliament and a Government to try to address the challenge that is inherent in different generations. That is to say that my parents may affix a certain definition and have a certain expectation of what the multiculturalism policy of the country ought to be doing. As a second generation Canadian I perhaps have a different expectation from a third or fourth generation Canadian. In addition to cultural retention perhaps, a third or fourth generation Canadian would also affix a political, economic and social expectation on the policy of the country.
I am not suggesting that one definition is wrong as compared to the other. What I am pointing to is that both definitions are valuable and relevant. Yet a different attitudi-nal approach is needed to provide a bridge between the various generations to ensure that the first generation and the second and third generations view the multiculturalism policy as a relevant instrument upon which to build a bigger, better and stronger Canada.
Therefore, I believe that the recommendation from the Youth Committee of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council is a
very wise one. I ask the Minister and government Members to consider supporting Motion No. 17, a motion which tries specifically to have federal institutions carve out a specific and effective program to address multiculturalism among the younger elements of our society.
The last amendment in my name is Motion No. 18. It would add subparagraph (g) to Clause 3. It suggests that federal Departments develop annual plans for the implementation of the multiculturalism policy and report on such plans in their annual reports.
The objective of this amendment is to try to commit federal Departments in a very specific way. If there is a role to play for our federal Departments, and clearly there is, in terms of enhancing and exercising all our policies and programs, then multiculturalism should not be an exception to the rule. We should not leave it there generally. We should try to apply it in a very specific way so that our federal Departments constructively and explicitly try to project a vision, an action plan, a series of priorities they would like to accomplish in any given year vis-a-vis multiculturalism.
It is not good enough to have a Department, a Minister, a departmental head or a Deputy Minister say: "We adhere to the general policy". Instead, they should be saying: "What can we be doing? What should we be doing as one Department to fulfil the goals and aspirations embodied in a multicultural policy in a multicultural Canada? How can we advance it one step further?"
The Government has chosen not to accept the concept of having an official multiculturalism commissioner, as there is with respect to official languages. There is a piece of legislation in place which was debated only last week which empowers an official commissioner who is able to monitor in order to try to ensure that the Civil Service and Crown corporations are adhering to the official bilingualism policy. The Government rejected the same type of approach with respect to multiculturalism. I regret that very much. I will be alluding to it in much greater detail in my speech on third reading.
Because the Government has not accepted that, I believe that the specific requirement for all Departments to have a yearly plan which would be submitted to Parliament and to the Minister is quite important. It would not carry out the function that would have been carried out by a commissioner such as the Official Languages Commissioner who is independent and who must report to Parliament. Notwithstanding that deficiency I believe it is incumbent upon us to say to the Departments: "If there is going to be a role, then let us tie it down. Let us ensure it is part of a coherent strategy plan within the Departments so that we as parliamentarians can address the various Departments to see where those annual reports are and therefore evaluate whether we are doing a job that is justified or whether we are doing a job that could be improved upon".
I am pleased that Parliament was able to agree with respect to the whole question of the fundamental characteristic which I addressed briefly only moments ago since I thought we were


only debating Motion No. 4. It is an important step. It is a step the Liberal Party tried to have recognized in the Meech Lake Accord when we moved one specific amendment. It was to have in the opening clause of our Constitution a recognition that our two official languages and our multicultural society constitute fundamental characteristics of the same country. To suggest one is fundamental and the other is an element really implies a different status for the two.
While we are not changing the constitutional Accord, and while this Party is still committed to negotiating a Meech Lake Accord that would see the opening clause proudly recognize multiculturalism as a fundamental characteristic, I am pleased that in Bill C-93 we are recognizing that multiculturalism constitutes a fundamental characteristic of our nation. It is my hope that we can go from this one specific clause in this piece of legislation and transfer that feeling and emotion into our Constitution the next time Parliament deals with the Meech Lake Accord.

Madam Speaker, I rise to support the amendments that are being discussed, particularly the amendments moved by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp).
It is not difficult for Governments to enunciate policies and for Governments to try to implement those policies by passing legislation. Unfortunately, experience and history have taught us that we can have a law and a policy, but if the determination to see that those policies are carried out is not very firm, then not much happens.
I remind Hon. Members that long before this Parliament or any of the provinces dealt with the question of multiculturalism the Parliament of Canada, and I believe almost every province in Canada, enacted after a great deal of discussion and after hearing many representations, fair employment practices legislation and fair accommodations legislation. The Parliament of Canada and the legislatures of Canada enunciated the principle that to discriminate in the fields of employment or housing against a person or persons because of their race, religion or colour and, later, sex, was contrary to the law. That sounds fine, but if one looks at the reality one sees that very little in fact has been accomplished.
If a study were made of Governments, federal, provincial or municipal, to see how many public servants employed by the three levels of government come from visible minority groups we would all hang our heads in shame. In my own City of Winnipeg I am certain that, if I examined the people who worked for the police and fire department, I could count on the fingers of my two hands the total number of people working for those two departments who come from visible minority groups.
Last week my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- North Centre (Mr. Keeper), was urging Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to use its influence to take action
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
against the owners of rental housing because there is a great deal of evidence that they discriminate in renting apartments to native people. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-North Centre, was correct in raising that matter. But I have to say with a good deal of dismay that I believe that not only was Canada Mortgage and Housing remiss, but so was the Manitoba Human Rights Commission, a commission set up in legislation in a province that has had an NDP Government for years. That commission should have been dealing with this question.
These are not easy matters. There is a great deal of prejudice among sections of our population. The whole point of that type of legislation, and the whole purpose of our attempt to deal with the reality of multiculturalism is to help the people from minority groups. My friend, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), stated that he is a first generation Canadian. I am a second generation Canadian. The fathers and grandfathers of some of the people whom I represent came to this country years ago, and some of the people I represent have come more recently in the last few years. They need assistance. They do not only need speeches telling them that we welcome them. They do not only need legislation which supposedly helps and protects them. What they need is real action on the part of Governments.
I say with a great deal of regret, and perhaps if I thought about it I could use much stronger language, that regardless of Party, Governments have not been as vigilant, as aggressive, and as determined as they should have been to deal with the type of discrimination that goes on.
Let me return to the debate when the Government brought in its Employment Equity Act. What is contained in the Act is fine as far as it goes, but the Act will be a failure because there is nothing in the Act that requires Departments to set targets, to attempt to reach those targets, and to report each year on how close they have come, or if they have come anywhere near to achieving the targets. If Departments are not implementing the policies that Governments have stated they believe in, then Governments can take the action to see that the type of principles set forth in that Employment Equity Act, and in the principles that are set forth in this Bill, become more than words in a Bill which gathers dust on the shelves of most law libraries in this country, but become a reality. Thai reality is extremely important and necessary for many people who live in this country.

Madam Speaker, I have a few words to say about this legislation, and I do wish to make a few points with regard to the motions that we are presently dealing with, particularly Motion No. 14 put forward by my colleague. This motion is designed to commit federal institutions to implementing policies, programs and practices rather than simply promoting them.
The reason this motion is significant is that in presenting this notion I hear my colleague saying that Governments ought to take action and not only have great rhetoric with regard to


Parklands
multiculturalism in Canada, and not only have the correct phrases when it comes to ethnic groups, but they ought to have programs that will make a real difference to the lives of people in the ethnic groups and communities in Canada. Some of the groups that exist in my riding have very high levels of employment, for example, the Philippine and Portuguese communities, and many other groups that are living in the inner city. Often members of those groups have professional qualifications acquired elsewhere which are not recognized in Canada. They have levels of unemployment that are unacceptable by Canadian standards and are certainly not reflected in the Canadian statistics that are issued and that become part of our television news.
Recently there was a report that unemployment in Canada is down to the lowest level in seven years. That is very impressive, but it is not the reality experienced by people in Winnipeg, in the inner City of Winnipeg, or in Winnipeg-North Centre. In ridings such as mine with very high levels of ethnic and immigrant groups, unemployment is more in the nature of 30 per cent rather than 6 per cent or 7 per cent, or whatever the official statistics are.
I do wish to compliment the Government with regard to its actions today. The Government has responded to the appeals from the ethnic and multicultural groups to put the words "fundamental characteristic" in the legislation, after much prodding from my colleague who is our critic in this area and prodding from the critic in the Liberal Party. The Government has seen the light and has introduced the words "fundamental characteristic" to describe multiculturalism rather than "fundamental element", whatever that was supposed to be.
I am pleased that the Government has responded to this prodding and has recognized that the multicultural nature of the country is a fundamental characteristic of the country. To me that means that we have a country and an ideal that respects the cultural heritage of each and every one of our citizens and groups, and that we have rejected the American notion of the "melting pot". We can have people preserve their language and culture and take pride in their origins. That is what "fundamental characteristic" means.
Now we have the ideal established, we need to get some muscle behind that ideal and at the level of the day-to-day lives of ordinary Canadians and new Canadians in order that it can make a difference in the type of jobs that they have, in the type of communities that they have, and in their equal access to opportunity and to a good life that they can enjoy in this country.
I must say that I welcome the fact that the Government has realized that it made a great deal of sense to put the words "fundamental characteristic" into the legislation. I am glad that the communities have had an opportunity to have their voices heard through the instrument of this Parliament. I hope this is only a first step and we will get down to very concrete programs. When ethnic groups and new Canadians are in the market-place, their qualifications will be recognized, their
opportunities for employment will be equal to those of any other Canadian, and they can look forward to an equal place on the Canadian stage, regardless of how long they have been in the country.
I understand that this multiculturalism Bill is a first, and it is long overdue. We welcome the fact that it is here today and being debated.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FEDERAL LANDS USE SUGGESTED DESIGNATION OF MILITARY LANDS AS POTENTIAL PARKLAND
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider designating as potential parkland all military lands located in urban areas and presently used for military purposes, once their present use is discontinued.
He said: Madam Speaker, you may be wondering why this motion is on the Order Paper and up for debate today. The motive and the instigation is caused by the fact that we do have across the nation a number of places where the land is being used for very appropriate and understandable purposes, including military purposes. In some large urban centres in Canada you have an area the size of an airport in the heart of the city, an area that is coveted and looked upon by a number of potentially interested parties, if and when the day will come for these lands to be abandoned for present use by the Department of National Defence.
My message is an environmental one, related to land use in urban Canada. I will put it very briefly along these lines. There will be pressures on our publicly-owned lands, which are at the present time under the administration of the Department of National Defence, as to when they should be declared vacant. The pressure will be enormous, particularly for additional housing, as indicated by my colleagues in this House in recent months. They have actually urged, particularly in the case of the city I come from, that the Downsview lands be used for housing purposes.
There could be pressure for other uses, such as commercial uses, and initiatives that would somehow indicate the desirability of the development of these lands. The alternative that I would propose in this motion is that these lands be designated at the appropriate time. I suppose this would have to be done in co-operation with the municipal and provincial authorities in order to designate them as parklands.


What does that mean? It is the concept of parkland in the broadest sense of the word. It would mean a use of these lands dedicated to environmental education, in relation to kids, in relation to schools and in relation to the public at large, on weekends. In other words, these would be demonstration areas where the biological characteristics and eco-systems of that particular region would be explained, and the number of environmental protection policies and programs would be explained at all levels. Therefore, you would have a centre in this particular park where the public would have an opportunity to absorb and to become acquainted with the science and practical application of environmental goals and objectives. It would not be such a bad idea, judging from the success that this idea has had in certain cities in Europe.
Second, the land that would be given up by the military authorities at the appropriate time could be used for conventional parkland, with the amenities that go with a park, which I do not have to describe at length.
Third, there could also be a combination or an addition or a parallel use of this land devoted to recreation, particularly in downtown areas where the densities are high, where there are large number of apartment dwellers and where the ratio of population to open space would be such that it would require this type of recreational land use.
Fourth, perhaps the ultimate in land use these days in an urban setting, where possible, is to devote such lands the creation of urban wildlife areas. We have, as you know, a wildlife that is retreating from the built-up areas, for understandable reasons. These wildlife areas may be possible where the size of the particular land is large enough. The size of a military airport is particularly suited for such a purpose. It may be a very interesting initiative to devote that particular public land to the development and the enshrinement of wildlife for the enjoyment of Canadians living in that region.
It is our use of land, if and when it becomes available, that has a very clear, specific purpose, namely, that of enhancing the quality of life in Canadian cities and in urban Canada in a manner that perhaps would make some of our cities unique in the world.
We have the space. We have the opportunity to do it. I would suggest that this would be a very imaginative way of contributing to the uniqueness of our cities. True, the pressures will be enormous in opposite directions. There will be those who will want additional housing, and it could make for a very strong social argument in their favour. I do not deny that. There will be those who will want commercial development. There will be those who will be able to propose some very interesting industrial land uses. Nevertheless, the purpose of this motion is centred around the notion of creating parklands in publicly-owned lands in our urban cities, because that is where the pressure is and where the transportation tie-ups already exist. That is where the pollution at times is high and where you would want to create open spaces for the benefit of citizens living in that particular area.
Parklands
I will stress it again, it is in our urban cities in the last two or three decades that we have seen a mushrooming of high-rise apartments, of high density dwellings, where the open spaces, the greenery, the yard, the front lawn of course exist only on a very minute surface, considering the number of people who live vertically above that specific property.
Therefore, the necessity of providing in certain urban centres additional open spaces cannot be denied, particularly if you come from Banff, like the Hon. Member across the aisle, or if you come from a community which is endowed with enormous amounts of open spaces, like Kapuskasing. I am talking of metropolitan centres that would include Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Calgary, Edmonton and Vancouver, to mention our larger urban centres.
Why would one take the trouble to make this point? In December of last year the then President of the Treasury Board, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), released a press communique on a federal lands study in Toronto. It put forward three concepts which I would like to examine quickly and put on record with which I find myself in partial agreement and then in total disagreement.

speechtext: How can you do that?

speechtext:
There are three, there is not one only. I will come to that.
The examination is limited only to federal lands in the Toronto region. It is a very interesting examination. The study is one which one no doubt must take seriously. I refer to the first page of the study where the main principles, the so-called guiding premises, are mentioned. The first one I find perfectly reasonable. It reads:
The federal Government will continue to hold lands that are appropriate to its operational needs.
There is nothing wrong with that. That is a way of having an insurance policy 100 years from now when these lands will become available. It may be that at that time the population pressures will be such as to enhance rather than diminish the chances for these lands to become open spaces, recreational areas, parkland, urban, wildlife or environmentally educational centres.
The second principle reads:
Lands not required for these purposes will be transferred to the appropriate jurisdictions or to other interests.
The words "other interests" trouble me a lot. I do not know how to interpret that. If it means a transfer from the federal level to a provincial or municipal level for public purposes, that is fine with me. I have no difficulty with that and I fully concur. But if it means transfer to private sector interests, then that is where we part company immediately.
The third principle reads:


Parklands
Where the federal Government agrees to transfer land, it is obligated to act in the best interest of Canada as a whole-
Which is just fine. There is no problem with that. Then, this is perhaps why I was bit unclear earlier. It goes on as follows:
-including seeking full value of the land on behalf of Canadian taxpayers.
The full value aspect, Mr. Speaker, troubles me enormously. If it means monetary value, as I suspect it does, then we part ways again. If it means that values are related to the enjoyment of landscapes, wildlife, trees and open spaces, there is no problem with that. If that full value implies monetary values, dollars and cents, then I submit there is no real way of arriving at a full value on behalf of Canadian taxpayers because some of this land has been increasing in value year after year, decade after decade. Only upon a sale does it reflect the value. That is not good enough when it comes to public land.
In an attempt to summarize the explanation for this motion before you and before my colleagues here today, Mr. Speaker, I would say that the study carried out by the consultants for the disposition of federal lands at a future date is welcome as an initiative. It is good that we find out what the major criteria should be. It is also a good thing that we debate this, which is what is taking place today. We should put our views on where we agree and where we do not.
I submit, as I have already, that land pressures in our metropolitan centres as the years go by will increase enormously. Hence we will have pressures for development in the conventional sense, as we know it, be it housing, commercial or industrial structures and buildings. I submit there is an alternative and there is a very good one. It relates to the necessity of having an alternative to the strong trend of building highrises, high density and the concentration of population on our limited urban land base.
We should make provision in the long term as one generation providing for subsequent generations-for those in the gallery, their children and grandchildren-with open spaces that they will enjoy. There is nothing more impressive than to go through a city that is heavily built up like Paris, Rome, my home City of Milan, Berlin, London, New York-you name it-and see what a limited and valuable commodity it is to come across open spaces in the form of parks. When they were established the parks may have been at the edges of a city and may have been surrounded or within a very small community. Now, instead, these parks are surrounded by highrises and are located in a major population centre. They are, therefore, such a strong contrast with the rest of the urban setting that they become green oases, for lack of a better word.
I am trying to argue this afternoon that we should project our thinking in the future and plan to make the military lands located in urban areas, when they become available, into green oases, open spaces for the enjoyment of generations of Canadians to come.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FEDERAL LANDS USE SUGGESTED DESIGNATION OF MILITARY LANDS AS POTENTIAL PARKLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate
in the debate on the Private Member's Motion today which has been put forward by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia).
Canadians take a well deserved pride in the beauty of our natural landscapes and in the history of our nation. The Hon. Member is to be congratulated for reminding the House of this fact. As a former Minister of the Environment, the Hon. Member knows that the Canadian Parks Service of Environment Canada is the federal agency whose clear mandate is to protect outstanding natural areas and historic places of national significance across Canada. Furthermore, he knows that the Canadian Parks Service plays a vital role in the preservation of our national heritage for present and future generations.
While we would all wish to expand Canada's national park system, Mr. Speaker, the present motion before the House would be both inappropriate and unnecessary. First, let us consider the nature of our national park system. Environment Canada, through its Canadian Parks Service, protects our national parks for all time because they are representative natural areas of Canadian significance. The national parks system encourages public understanding, appreciation and enjoyment of this natural heritage so as to leave it unimpaired for future generations. You should note, Mr. Speaker, the emphasis on the word natural. To be suitable for consideration as a national park, an area must have experienced minimal modification by humans or, if significant change has taken place, it must have potential for restoration to a natural state. Military lands in urban areas would simply not meet these criteria.
I was surprised to hear the Hon. Member talk about the Downsview airport which is located practically in the centre of Metropolitan Toronto in the North York section. It seems to me that the area in Metro Toronto that should be preserved and is in that wild state now is the Rouge Valley and not the Downsview airport which is more appropriate for housing.
The Hon. Member said that there should be urban wildlife. The motto of the Save the Rouge System is: "Wild in the City". Indeed, there is a whole herd of white-tailed deer running through Metro Toronto, if you can believe that, Mr. Speaker. We want the deer to be preserved wild in the city.
In fact, it is self-evident that in all of Canada, the places the furthest removed from their natural states are urban military areas. Military lands located in urban areas would certainly not qualify for inclusion in our national parks system based on the essential criteria of sights representing unspoiled natural beauty.
However, the Canadian Parks Service, through its National Historic Parks and Sites Program, may designate and commemorate areas of national historic interest. This is accomplished only upon the recommendation of the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada, which is the advisory body


in such matters for the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan). To be selected for such commemoration, a place must be associated with an event or a movement which has shaped Canadian history, and/or illustrate effectively the culture of a pre-historic people or be associated with important archaeological discoveries.
Only places of extraordinary value to Canadian history are acquired and developed as national historic parks. All military lands are not intrinsically of national historic significance. They are not, nor should they be, automatically eligible for national commemoration.
This process is as it should be right now. Truly worthy sites of genuine national historic significance can be and are considered by the Historic Sites and Monuments Board. When these sites meet the proper criteria, they are given the appropriate designation. The system has worked and is working very well indeed. There is no need to tinker with it now, nor was there such a need when the Hon. Member who moved this motion served as Minister of the Environment.
To date, there has been excellent co-operation between the Department of National Defence and Environment Canada. DND is fully aware of Environment Canada's interest in and mandate for maintaining land of national historic significance. DND has routinely co-operated in the past by transferring to Environment Canada historically significant lands that were no longer required for military purposes.
In fact, military lands are already exceedingly well represented in Canada's historic parks system. DND has already transferred to the Canadian Parks Service some of the most important military sites in Canada. In fact, Canada's whole system of national historic parks and major historic sites began in 1917 with the transfer of Fort Anne in Nova Scotia from the Department of Militia and Defence to what was then the National Parks Service. Fort Anne was the first of our national historic parks.
From Signal Hill in St. John's, Newfoundland-where the final battle of the Seven Years War in North America was fought on September 15, 1762-to Fort Rodd Hill in Victoria, British Columbia-where batteries were constructed in 1895 as part of a coastal system to defend Esquimalt and Victoria- military sites, literally from one end of Canada to the other, have been preserved and are appreciated by hundreds of thousands of Canadians and foreign visitors each and every year.
Indeed, when it comes to military historic sites, Canada has been blessed. Seventeenth, 18th and 19th-century military history is well preserved and represented by national historic parks and sites. When one adds provincial sites to the list of federal lands of this type, we can proudly say that this aspect of history remains a living heritage accessible to all Canadians.
As all Hon. Members can see, it is clear that it would be totally inappropriate to turn over urban sites owned by the Department of National Defence for use as national parks
Parklands
because their value as unspoiled natural areas has been irredeemably debased. They would add nothing to our system of national historic sites which already include impeccable and comprehensive representations of our 17th, 18th and 19th-century military history.
Hon. Members can be assured that this Government will continue to ensure the preservation of nationally significant examples of Canada's military history as we have done so well in the past. For all these reasons, the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Davenport is inappropriate and should be rejected by Hon. Members of the House of Commons.

Madam
Speaker, I was not sure whether or not I would support the motion put by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) until I heard the Parliamentary Secretary. She confirmed in my mind why I should support the motion, and I will tell her why in a minute.

I personally do not think that the two are necessarily in conflict, but sometimes they can be partly in conflict. I have some concerns about that.
I thought that the Parliamentary Secretary was too bureaucratic and that there was too much of the DND in her response. I thought she mixed up the notion of national historic sites and national military sites, of all things, with what the Hon. Member for Davenport was trying to deal with. The Hon. Member for Davenport mentioned the use of lands under a number of criteria. He mentioned using land as an environmental centre, as conventional parkland, as a recreational centre, as a wildlife centre or as all of these. He suggested that we could use these military lands that are no longer used for military purposes for environmental purposes, but for different kinds of environmental purposes.
I do not think that the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary should dismiss this motion so quickly. She said that perhaps Downs-view airport is more suitable for housing than it is for parkland

and she said that we should look to the Rouge Valley. I believe that is in the Hon. Member's riding, is it not?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FEDERAL LANDS USE SUGGESTED DESIGNATION OF MILITARY LANDS AS POTENTIAL PARKLAND
speechtext:
I knew there was a lot of wildlife in Toronto, as the Hon. Member said. As a matter of fact, we have a little saying in Vancouver. Of course, I do not subscribe to it. They say: "They don't call it Hogtown for nothing". It is nice to know they have some deer and that everyone is not in a fervent rush to make money. When I think of Toronto, I do not think of Bambi, I think more of Godzilla. However, it is nice to know.
Here is where the Parliamentary Secretary is wrong. She said there were precedents for taking military land. She mentioned that the DND transferred military land to parks, so we have precedents. Let us not confuse it with military sites, though. I would rather have environmental sites, quite frankly, than more military sites. We would have more sites commemorating militarism. While we have to commemorate our past, the reality of military battles, let us not go overboard. My feeling was that DND would tend to want to have more military sites than environmental parks, so let us not dismiss the Member's motion. I think he has a good idea.
To give you an example. In my home City of Vancouver, right near where I used to live, there is a park called Jericho Beach. It was an active military site, and still is, although it is empty now. It was used during the war. You can see pictures of the old hangars and military barracks and so on. It is right on the ocean, just outside of English Bay, towards Point Grey and the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, a beautiful area. As a matter of fact, it was used for the Habitat Conference. The Hon. Member for Davenport mentioned an environmental centre. It was used as a people centre for the Habitat Conference 10 or 15 years ago. That was the beginning of the Stockholm environmental notion and the things we are dealing with today. We did a good job in Vancouver in having it there.
The other thing about Jericho Beach is that it has areas for recreation. I used to jog around there myself when I was in better shape before I came to Parliament and got out of shape. It was a good area to jog around. There was wildlife there and
even the military people who were looking after it allowed some bogs and areas like that to continue to exist. They did not develop it all. There was and is wildlife today, bird flyways and so on. You have urban wildlife, the real kind, that is, animals and birds. That is a good example, and therefore I do not think the Parliamentary Secretary should decide this out of hand and take the bureaucratic line from DND. I think this is something worth looking into.
I congratulate the Hon. Member for Davenport because he is a former Minister of the Environment who has always had his heart in the right place on environmental issues. However, I wish he had enumerated in more detail the number of these military sites. He mentioned Downsview. I have seen Downs-view from the air while flying across Toronto and I wonder what it is being used for. I would like to know the future plans for that area. I wish the Hon. Member had named some of the other sites across Canada because there may be other areas available. Let us enumerate them, let us see what uses they could be put to.
He also mentioned the report done by the Government on the federal land study in Toronto. I, too, have my concerns. We have a Conservative Government that likes to privatize government property for its friends in the private sector. It is a Government that you cannot trust. For example, it made promises to seniors that it would not deindex their pensions, and then turned around and tried to do just that. It made a promise there would be no free trade. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said he was against it, and then he brought in free trade. So it is a Government you cannot trust.

Madam Speaker, my point simply is that many of us, not just me, but many others in the country do not trust the Government to deal straightforwardly with matters. One of the problems in dealing with these particular lands is the federal land study in Toronto. We are concerned that instead of putting them to environmental or other uses such as housing, the Government might sell them to its friends. Let us look at the record. Look at the past. Look at what the Government has done.
I want to conclude by saying this. I think the Hon. Member for Davenport has made a good start. We really should look at and analyse these military lands. We should make the environment, whether it is a centre, a parkland, a recreation, urban wildlife or combination of them all, an important use. We have to weigh the housing usage factor. We have to weigh the use for commercial purposes and environmental purposes. I agree with the Hon. Member. I think the time has come to restrict urban growth and create more open spaces and enhance the existing ones in urban areas. That will enhance the quality of life, which is what we are all trying to do and what we are proud of having as Canadians. That is why I think


this is a very creative motion and it deserves a better look than the Parliamentary Secretary was prepared to give.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate today on Motion 164 moved by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia).
Madam Speaker, this motion by a former Minister of the Environment, well-intentioned though it may be, comes somewhat as a surprise. In any case, since the Hon. Member for Davenport must be aware of the federal policies relating to the Canadian parks system, he might have refrained from presenting this kind of motion.
Perhaps the Hon. Member is worried that Canada's military heritage is under-represented in our network of national historic parks.
Future generations need not worry. Since the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada was established in 1919, the number of historic sites, parks, monuments and canals has steadily increased. Since 1917, several old forts administered by the Army has been transferred to the National Historic Parks Branch.
Madam Speaker, perhaps I may recall that in the fifties, the federal Government has focused its attention on a number of sites, most of which were former military centres.
In fact, from the outset, co-operation between the Department of National Defence and the department responsible for national parks was always excellent, and it still is today. Thanks to this mutual understanding, from the early settlement of this country to the beginning of the twentieth century, all across this country from Signal Hill, Newfoundland to Fort Rodd Hill, British Columbia, our national historic parks are a faithful reflection of the relationship between our country's history and its various regions. These parks give Canadians and foreign visitors a good picture of our military history in the 17th, 18th and 19th centuries.
Madam Speaker, the motion in its present form does not specify the historic value of these lands and fails to make any distinctions. In view of existing provisions for having any site of national historic significance taken into consideration, and since the motion fails to consider the value of the lands in question, a motion of this kind is useless as far as the preservation of our country's heritage is concerned.
It is not useful to create national parks, Madam Speaker, since it ignores the objectives and criteria of Environment Canada in this respect.
The purpose of creating national parks is to safeguard natural areas that are representative of this country so as to keep them intact for future generations.
It does not seem necessary to me to sustantiate for the House the fact that the motion introduced by the Hon.
Parklands
Member for Davenport does not meet the criterion of geographic representativeness; it also goes without saying that a former Minister of the Environment should know that military lands located in urban areas are far removed from the definition of a natural area. I ask you, Madam Speaker, what could be less natural than a city?
It remains passing strange, Madam Speaker, that this former Minister of the Environment, who has done so much for our common heritage could have drafted such a motion.
Canada has one of the most beautiful networks of national parks in the world. At the present time, this network comprises 34 national parks disseminated throughout our vast land. They cover 1.3 percent of Canada's overall territory.
Since this Government came to power, we have signed agreements and spent millions of dollars for the creation of new parks, such as at Moresby South in the Queen Charlotte Islands, on the Bruce Peninsula in Ontario, on Ellesmere Island in the Arctic, and more recently, in the Saguenay region in Quebec.
In Quebec, our historical military heritage is far from being under-represented. For instance, we have Fort Lennox on l'ile-aux-Noix, Battlefield Park and the walled fortifications of Quebec in the City of Quebec, Fort No. 1 of Pointe-Levis in Lauzon, the Chateauguay Battlements in Howick, and Chambly Fort in Chambly. All of these parks and historical sites bear witness to the military history of past regimes.
The public has shown a growing interst in such sites, and thousands of our fellow Canadians, as well as tourists from all over the world, seek them out for their beauty and for their historical interest.
We can assure the Canadian population that we are continuing and will continue to work for the preservation of our heritage and that we will also continue to improve our national parks network and our national historical parks.
Unfortunately, Madam Speaker, motion 164 introduced by the Hon. Member for Davenport is far from meeting the objectives which underly the creation of national parks and national historical parks, nor can it influence municipalities or provincial governments to preserve green spaces.
For all of these reasons, Madam Speaker, we suggest that the motion be defeated by this honorable House.
