Madam Speaker, I would like to say just a few words in support of Motion No. 164, on behalf of my colleague from Davenport (Mr. Caccia). I think that this motion raises some very important issues for people living in urban areas who have military facilities that are obsolete or declared surplus for government requirements and that must be redeveloped either for housing or in accordance with some municipal projects or


Parklands
plans or that are to be used for roads or other purposes for all municipalities in the region.
I raise the matter because, first of all, it is of current interest in Ottawa-Vanier and, second, it has always concerned me. How are federal lands that are declared surplus disposed of and how are lands that were used for military purposes disposed of not only for the development of communities that identify with those facilities or have had to live with them for many years, but also how can nature parks and other natural areas, which everyone considers very important, be planned for our urban centres? There is a great need to maintain green spaces that everyone can enjoy and to give municipalities a chance to develop within their territory a place where people can do other things than playing war games.
Madam Speaker, Motion No. 164 from the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider designating as potential parkland all military lands located in urban areas and presently used for military purposes, once their present use is discontinued.
So this is a recommendation that the Government should take seriously and put on the agenda to see whether urban areas do require more facilities to meet public needs, before dismissing it entirely.
You know, Madam Speaker, in my riding, there is a property known as . . .

-DND property on Lees Avenue. It is known as the Armories property. I understand that some years ago this property was designated as surplus to federal needs in terms of military installations. Therefore, everyone and his neighbour has had his eyes on it and planning has been going on to take this property to serve transportation needs or other regional requirements. Much to my dismay no one in Government has seriously suggested that it be used for ecological environment parks or, even better, in downtown Ottawa, some good affordable housing.
This dossier has been with us for some time. Just for the sake of making it known that we do have a few sites in Ottawa Vanier which have been declared surplus, and in whose interest it is that they be preserved for public use, there are plans to declare the federal property known as the Armories as surplus and to transfer that property to the regional Government for a major road project through the area proposed by the regional municipality.
I wish to refer to a letter from the Alderman Nancy Smith of St. George's Ward, written to me on January 29, 1988. She says:
I am writing you with regard to the DND property on Lees Avenue, otherwise known as the Armories property. It would appear that this property may become surplus in the near future.
She goes on to say that the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton may have access to that property to realign some of its road patterns in the area. She continues:
The land in this area is zoned for residential. In particular, the DND site
was reviewed at the time of the Ottawa East Neighbourhood Plan (1979 to
1980). It is zoned for family housing with a 35 foot to 45 foot height limit.
She went on to explain how important it is that there should be housing on that property.
The Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) stated that he would like to see any surplus federal lands now used for military purposes, when they became surplus declared to be environmental parks. 1 do not disagree with him that there is a need for environmental parks, but on that point I might debate his argument. There are some cities where there are several such military properties. I can think of at least two in my riding. The site on Lees Avenue, known as the Armouries site, could be used for good quality housing while giving the residents of Ottawa East a park at the same time. In other words, we could easily cope with both the housing requirements of the community and the park requirements of the children and residents of that area.
This is a good motion. It appeals to me because of its human approach to disposing of properties that the federal Government no longer needs. This could easily be taken up by the Government, to consider how the various cities, towns and urban areas where properties used for DND purposes that were declared surplus could be converted into parks or, for that matter, a mix of parks and housing. If that is the purpose at hand, then it has the full approval of all residents of Ottawa- Vanier.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate today. I congratulate the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), a former Minister of Environment, for his interest.
I want to take this opportunity to point out what I genuinely feel are a few imperfections in what he is proposing. As a former Minister of the Environment, the Hon. Member for Davenport should know that this motion is neither feasible nor practical. The very wording of the motion, the way in which it is drafted, seems to fly in the face of government policies, both of this Government and of previous ones, for parks designation and for the disposal of surplus lands.
Let us look at the phrase "considered designated as potential parkland". The motion does not explain what this phrase means, nor does it say how such a goal can be achieved in law.
At present there is no provision either in the laws governing the selection or acquisition of our national parks, or in the parks policy of the Canadian Parks Service, for the designation of an area as potential parkland. After an area is selected for consideration as a national parkland on the basis of well defined criteria, it is either designated a park or it is not. There is no such thing now, nor has there ever been a designation for potential parkland.


Let us consider the selection procedure for designating a Canadian national historic site. This selection process is carried out by the National Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada. A site, which may have national significance, either as a location in its own right or in relation to a person or event of Canada-wide importance, is nominated for consideration by the board.
Nowhere in this process, which has been working smoothly and efficiently since 1919, is provision made for a designation as potential parkland.
Likewise, Motion No. 164 refers to parkland rather than national parkland or land for national parks. The mandate of the Canadian Parks Service concerns the establishment of national parks; that is, the establishment of parks as areas that have true national significance as a result of their superlative natural characteristics and unspoiled state. Surely a former Minister of the Environment should be expected to realize that the chances of any urban military land qualifying under the rigid criteria for national parks are extremely remote, to say the least.
Since this is the case, the Hon. Member for Davenport must be implying by the omission of the word "national" that the surplus land intended for designation as potential parkland is intended for municipal or provincial parkland. Surely it is not the role of the federal Government to tell other levels of government what they should or should not designate as parkland, either potential or not. If such a designation is meant to apply to urban areas for consideration by the federal Government as parkland it is meaningless, if it is meant to apply to provincial or local governments it is presumptuous.
The proposal of the Hon. Member for Davenport to designate surplus urban land of the Department of National Defence as potential parkland is simply not feasible. Moreover, it is unnecessary. There is a formal disposal process already in place to handle surplus DND land, and indeed all surplus land of the federal Government.
If the intent of Motion No. 164 is simply to designate surplus urban DND land as parkland in order to alleviate shortages of green space in urban areas, then the Hon. Member for Davenport could have perhaps stated his goal more clearly. In that case, however, he might have confronted the reality that municipal and provincial Governments already have the opportunity to obtain federal Government land once it is declared surplus. If they decide surplus DND lands are required for parks there already exist adequate and functional procedures to obtain such lands.
The intent of Motion No. 164 is clear, to say the least. As a measure to augment our national parks system it cannot work, because urban lands are unsuitable for use as national parks; as an instrument to improve the selection of historic parks and sites it is unnecessary; and as a means of increasing municipal urban green space it is inappropriate and ineffectual.
Parklands
Canada's national parks system is one of the great glories of our country. Our national parks are a means of preserving, in their natural state, areas which are representative of the major natural environments of Canada. They are special places which protect part of the heritage of all Canadians, now and in the future. The first national park in Canada was established in 1885 to protect the then newly discovered Banff Hot Springs for public use. Now, our national park system encompasses 34 parks, which cover 1.3 per cent of Canada's entire land mass.
The official policy of the Canadian Parks Service sets as a goal the representation of each land and marine natural region of Canada by a national park or marine national park. However, many land and most marine natural regions are still unrepresented. This is a worth-while goal which this Government is diligently and constantly pursuing.
The present Government is proud to have added a significant number of new national parks to Canada's national parks system during the years of its tenure. Bruce Peninsula and Ellesmere Island are the new national parks or national park reserves the Government has recently created. Canadians can be assured that the Government will continue to build on this record of success and show leadership in continuing to improve Canada's national park system.
Unfortunately, Motion No. 164 will not bring us any closer to reaching any of these goals, nor can it possibly have any practical or additional impact on the preservation of urban green space by municipal or provincial Governments.
Notwithstanding the items I pointed out, I still congratulate the Hon. Member for his interest in the environment. Both my colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Browes), and I have worked diligently on behalf of the Save the Rouge campaign in eastern Metro Toronto. We are sympathetic to all worth-while suggestions regarding the environment. Unfortunately, Motion No. 164 does not appear to be the vehicle for the end result that is actually sought by the Hon. Member.

That Bill C-93 be amended in Clause 6 by striking out lines 27 to 31 at page 6 and substituting the following therefor:

He said: Madam Speaker, this group of motions is designed to clarify the responsibilities of the Minister responsible for multiculturalism and other members of the Cabinet in acting on the statement of principles which Clause 3 has set forth so well in the Bill, but which in the draft that came to the House and in the Bill that came back to the House from the legislative committee still leaves all too much opportunity for individuals to act on the policy or to ignore the policy.
Because of the nature of these provisions, I provide as an example Clause 5, the first paragraph of which provides that the Minister shall take such measures as the Minister considers appropriate to implement the multiculturalism policy of Canada without limiting the generality, and so on. Then some specific statements are made. That particular phrase, "shall take such measures as the Minister considers appropriate", has impressed a great many people as opening the possibility to failing to respect the principles set forth in Clause 3, as opening the door to ignoring the multicultural policy, something which many observers seem to think has characterized government Departments far too often.
The need to strengthen various clauses of the Bill was recognized by the Canadian Ethnocultural Council in its own presentation on the matter which, under the title "Strengthening the Act, a Brief on Bill C-93", was made public in April of this year and said among other things in specific reference to Clause 5, paragraph (1):
The opening paragraph of Section 5(1) could be worded in a more definitive manner as follows: "The Minister shall take measures appropriate to


Canadian Multiculturalism Act
implement the multicultural policy of Canada and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, may"
Similar suggestions have come forth for other clauses. Looking at Clause 4 of the Bill, the Canadian Ethnocultural Council has suggested that there might be a broadening of the ambit of the Bill by stating that the Minister, all other Ministers of the Crown, and all federal institutions shall implement the multiculturalism policy of Canada. It has been my response to these suggestions to put forward this series of motions, all of which deal in one way or another with ministerial obligation.
Motion No. 20 gives the Minister an active role by himself and with his cabinet colleagues. Motion No. 21, as I have already said, removes from Clause 5 any excuse for inaction and commits the Minister to ongoing consultation with ethnocultural communities and multicultural organizations.
I need hardly say that organizations nationally and provincially have been very concerned about the need for such close consultation. They have all too often been promised consultation by Ministers and then have not seen it actually carried out. Again, with its basis for the implementation of multicultural policy, I have endeavoured in Motion No. 21 to place that obligation on the Ministers so that they will actually realize, having read the Act once it is proclaimed, that these are the requirements of the position.
Motion No. 24 amends Clause 5 in order to ensure consultation with provincial and territorial Governments. I do not think it is any secret that the first federal-provincial meeting of Ministers responsible for multiculturalism, a meeting which the Hon. Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) carried out as the first multiculturalism Minister of this Conservative Government, was thought by people in some of the provinces as a very important meeting in forcing provincial Governments to give attention to multiculturalism and in encouraging them to press on with the elaboration of their own policies. Recognizing from our side that this policy of 1971 needs to be pushed on in the various jurisdictions of Canada, an obligation to have such meetings with provincial and territorial Governments could be of great value.
Finally, in Motions Nos. 25 and 26 I have attempted to amend Clause 6 in order to strengthen the obligations of all Ministers of the Crown to advance the multiculturalism policy. In Motion No. 26 I have attempted, again deliberately, to ensure that Ministers' Departments develop annual plans designed to ensure that the multiculturalism policy, to which lip service is so often paid politically, and to which governments have ostensibly been committed for many years past, is actually achieved in practice and becomes the basis for action in the various Departments of the Government.
These various motions are designed to strengthen the Bill and ensure it is a reality for the federal Government.

Madam Speaker, I would like to address two motions of the group that I proposed on behalf of the Liberal Party, that is to say, Motions Nos. 22 and 23. Before doing that, I would like to say that I support my friend's Motion No. 26 in that it is very similar to the motion I moved earlier, a motion which was ultimately defeated, to try to get Ministers and their Departments to develop annual plans to foster and enhance multiculturalism not in broad general strokes but in very specific and tangible ways.
With respect to Motion No. 22, in essence it seeks to change very weak wording to very strong and committed wording. Clause 5 of the Bill talks about ministerial obligations. It says the Minister "may" take such measures as the Minister considers appropriate to implement the multiculturalism policy of Canada, and so on. I propose here, as I have in other areas of the Bill, to change the word "may" to "shall".
Some Members might think that is nit-picking. Some people might think that it is being too particular. I suggest it is not. From the opening paragraph to the closing paragraph of the Bill we have a lot of words which should have been changed to make the Bill more forceful, more secure, more tangible. We should avoid talking about doing something or wanting something done, and instead ensure that it will be done. It has to be seen as an obligation on the part of the Minister to fulfil a number of multiculturalism policies that I concur in. However, if the language suggests that the Minister "may" do it if he or she wants to, then you have a situation where one Minister of one Party will do it and a subsequent Minister of the same Party or of a different Party may not. That leads to inconsistencies and differences in the implementation of programs. The language in the Bill is crucial if we are to maintain consistency, commitment, and national standards.
Motion No. 23 refers to Clause 5 of the Bill which says again the Minister "may" enter into an agreement or arrangement with any province respecting implementation of the multiculturalism policy of Canada. My motion would have the Bill say that the Minister "shall" engage in ongoing dialogue with all provinces and territories respecting implementation of the multiculturalism policy of Canada and so on.
There are two key points to this motion. The first one concerns changing "may" to "shall". The first conference called by the then Minister, the Hon. Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta), was I believe held in 1985. There have been no other meetings since then. It would have been very valuable and productive to have had a commitment to annual meetings of First Ministers on such an important issue. As it was, it was a one-day wonder and nothing was produced. There was no tangible follow up to that meeting. Had there been another set of meetings in 1986, 1987 and again this year there would have been action on a number of priority items. As it was, it was an initiative by one Minister that simply went nowhere.
The second point of my motion concerns the territories. Right now the legislation stops at provinces. I note that the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Weiner) is in the


House right now and I applaud him for being here. I ask him to consider adding the word "territories" to the Bill. I ask myself, why leave out two territories when we are talking about a national policy? We sometimes hear calls from the wilderness, if you will, where people feel that they are being left out of the process. There is some justification for that feeling, particularly when we look at the Meech Lake Accord and other issues. This is a case in point. The legislation speaks only to arrangements on multiculturalism with the provinces. I suggest it would be in keeping with this country's history to include the territories in any discussion of multiculturalism.
I hope the Minister and his Government recognize the failure, and I am not saying it was intentional, perhaps oversight is a better word, in leaving the territories out. I ask the Government to remedy that by including the territories in discussions with the provinces.

Motion No. 28.
That Bill C-93 be amended in Clause 7 by striking out lines 37 to 45 at page 6 and substituting the following therefor:
"7.(1) The Minister shall establish an Advisory Council to assist the Minister and Government in implementation of this Act and any other matter relating to the multiculturalism policy of Canada.
(2) The members of the Advisory Council shall be appointed by order in council from nominees elected by the various ethnocultural communities and national multicultural organizations."

Madam Speaker, I would like to address my remarks to Motion No. 27, which is one of the last two amendments at report stage. Motion No. 27 refers to the section in the Bill which addresses the Canadian Multiculturalism Council. The CMC, or the advisory committee, is a body established by the Government to advise the Minister of the


day on issues affecting the multicultural policy of the country. I have proposed a much more description and, I believe, a much more effective direction to the CMC as it now is.
Clause 7(1) of the Bill says:
The Minister may establish an advisory committee to advise and assist the Minister on the implementation of this Act and any other matter relating to multiculturalism and, in consultation with such organizations representing multicultural interests as the Minister deems appropriate, may appoint the members and designate the chairman and other officers thereof.
The language is noncommittal. The word "may" is used which does not commit the Minister to any specific action. A different approach to implementation may be taken by subsequent Ministers, thereby confusing the entire CMC as we know it today.
In addition to proposing in Motion No. 27 that "the Minister shall establish a council to advise and assist the Minister", I go to some length in proposing the shape of the Canadian Multiculturalism Advisory Council, the number of members, the issue of an executive committee, the fact that the membership should reflect the diversity of the Canadian mosaic, and that appointments should be made from lists submitted by the various organizations across the country in order to ensure that the people appointed to this committee will reflect the diversity which exists in Canada and will be in touch with the communities which they purport to represent.
These amendments reflect the proposals which were made for the Canadian Multiculturalism Advisory Committee by the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism which the Government rejected.
It is particularly important that we have an executive comprised of one member from each province. This will eliminate having a large organization coming to Ottawa to meet and advise the Minister. I do not think that large numbers are as effective as a smaller group. In Motion No. 27 I suggest that the council be formed of the 56 members which I propose: seven from British Columbia, four from Alberta, three from Saskatchewan, four from Manitoba, 16 from Ontario, 12 from Quebec, two from New Brunswick, two from Nova Scotia, two from Prince Edward Island, two from Newfoundland, one from the Yukon, and one from the Northwest Territories. I recommend that only one member from each province and territory form an executive to come to Ottawa. This will reduce the expense and will enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of that body.
The other important element is that appointments by the Minister to the Canadian Advisory Council on Multiculturalism should be rooted in the large number of organizations which are working on behalf of multiculturalism across the country. It is now alleged, unfortunately, that many of the appointments tend to be very political and partisan. In fact the Vice-President, Mr. Peter McCreath, acknowledged, in a paper to which I will be alluding later, that the current CMC is nothing more than an appendix of the current Government.
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
I am not suggesting that that kind of political partisanship did not take place in previous administrations-it did. I am suggesting that we should rise above that in order to appoint people who can enhance and propel the policy of multiculturalism in the future. I am not suggesting that the current membership of the existing CMC is not interested in multiculturalism. However, there is a perception in the country that they tend toward having a political partisan base.
There is a real concern that members who are appointed to this committee to represent one cultural group or community are not known to that group or community. They ask what is the purpose of having a committee of individuals who are not rooted in the actual communities and cultural groups themselves to advise the Minister and the Government. I believe my amendment would attempt to redress that perception which has existed for a number of years. Our obligation is to eradicate that perception. In that way we will build confidence and a positive perception of government institutions.
Motion No. 27 is an attempt to go beyond the proposition in Bill C-93, to make it more of a commitment so that the Minister will, rather than perhaps, appoint a committee. It is an attempt to root the membership from actual membership lists provided by groups and organizations across the country. It provides for a specific membership allotted to the provinces and territories and that there be an executive committee.
If we follow this course, I believe we will be in better tune with the workings of government machinery and in better tune and synchronization with the aspirations of communities across this country.
Hopefully the Government will see the benefit of such a proposition, which was included in the unanimous report of the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism which urged the Government to reform the area of the advisory committee in a very real and profound way so as to remove the very negative way many people viewed the appointment of individuals to an important body.

Madam Speaker, the last two motions before us for debate deal with the constitution of an advisory body to the Government, particularly to the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Weiner). This is a matter of great importance. Given the changes that have occurred in the Bill, presumably on the suggestion of the Minister or the will of government Members, it is particularly important to deal with this matter in a responsible way.
I recognize that the motions with which we were dealing a few moments ago deal with the commitment of the Minister of Multiculturalism's policy and that Conservative caucus members believe the Bill does not need to be strengthened in those areas. However, I want to ask some serious questions of the Minister and seek to persuade him and his colleagues of the possibility of changing their minds on this matter.


Canadian Multiculturalism Act
When the Bill first came to the House, Clause 7 read: "The Minister may establish a council to advise and assist the Minister on the implementation of this Act and any other matter relating to multiculturalism". When the committee considered this particular clause in the Bill, the Conservative members, who were the only ones present that afternoon, decided to change "council" to an "advisory committee". Frankly, the logic for that never became clear to me. It might be worth the Minister's taking a few moments to explain why an advisory committee would be a preferable change.
The Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) already referred to the long history of a consultative committee on multiculturalism. It became the multicultural council, and the present council has been advising Ministers for some years. While its members have been reappointed and some new ones added since the Government took office in 1984, there has been a good deal of continuity from its first constitution to the present one. It has been an advisory council throughout this period and, admittedly, it has tended to be perilously close to the Minister's pocket in many ways.
It has rarely said anything in public. I believe the only time the multiculturalism council to the present Government said anything in public was when it decided to, I might say, shoot its mouth off in support of the Government's failure to act on Japanese Canadian redress. Many Canadians would regard that as a rather lamentable statement.
While it has done important things for Government, it has not really lived up to the advisory council nature that one would have expected.
Perhaps the Minister is suggesting that since the council does not do much it may as well be turned into an advisory committee, to make it even more in house. The Member for York West quoted, in a document sent to a previous Minister, the vice-chairman's description of the Canadian Multicultural Council as being all Tories working for the re-election of the Government. I want to say quite advisedly that I do not believe that is true of all the members of the CMC. I am certain some of them are not card-carrying members of the Conservative Party, but are members who are really committed to multiculturalism and for whom the re-election of the Government is less important, if I may say, than the realization of the multicultural policy. I suggest that to change the multiculturalism council to an advisory committee seems a rather serious demotion.
What alternatives exist? We are dealing here with two motions. The Member for York West has spoken well to his proposal. I was involved in the elaboration of that proposal as a member of the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism. Obviously, I think his motion is quite good.
I chose not to become involved in the details of numbers and constitution concerned with executive committee and so on. As a member of the standing committee I am not withdrawing my support from those detailed proposals with which the standing committee dealt, and will likely support this motion. In my
motion, however, I endeavoured to turn the advisory council to the Minister into a council that would be explicitly advisory to the Minister and to government.
Let me take a moment to read Clause 7 in part as it would read if my motion were accepted. Clause 7(1) would read:
The Minister shall establish an Advisory Council to assist the Minister and Government in implementation of this Act and any other matter relating to the multiculturalism policy of Canada.
Clause 7(2) would read:
The members of the Advisory Council shall be appointed in order in council from nominees elected by the various ethnocultural communities and national multicultural organizations.
There is a deliberate attempt in the first paragraph to establish a body that will be advisory to the whole Government, not simply to the Minister. I think that would make it a more public body than has been true of the consultative councils on multiculturalism before and the present multiculturalism council as such. In considering such a body, we might have an expectation of something like the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. In fact, I thought quite explicitly of that model in another area. In that case, of course, there were national organizations which thought it advisable to have an action committee in communities and nationally to ensure that the Government was sufficiently pressed. However, the Advisory Council on the Status of Women has had research capacity. It has, I believe, a full time chairperson and staff who carry on the work. I think that provides a model which is really far preferable than an advisory committee as presently stated in the Bill.
With respect to the second paragraph, I have been quite concerned to ensure this body would relate to the communities. Whether people were all Liberals in the past and all Conservatives now, and I do not suppose it would be either of those situations, what was, I fear, all too often the case was that persons, for whatever reason-primarily, I suppose, they had to be known to the politicians-did not necessarily translate into being well positioned in the communities and well aware of what the people wanted. There was in fact quite a real danger that the persons who made up this so-called advisory council to Government were not equipped in their experience and involvement to be the best of advisers to Government.
Therefore in both of these motions, and in the report of the standing committee, there is an attempt to ensure that these persons will be nominated by the communities and, of course, appointed by Order in Council of the Government of Canada to constitute such an advisory body. In fact, in the case of the Manitoba Intercultural Council there is precisely such a body. The majority of the members of the Manitoba Intercultural Council are in fact members of that council on precisely this basis. That ensures that the council is well grounded in the communities and equipped to speak for them, which I think is the all important thing.


I hope the Minister may comment at least briefly on his own vision of the advisory committee. If the arguments my colleague and I have been making for a different structure were to impress him, perhaps he would be interested in taking up one or the other proposal as he has done once or twice already this afternoon.

behalf of the Secretary of State, moved that Bill C-93, an Act for the preservation and enhancement of multiculturalism in Canada, be concurred in as amended.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Minister of State on a point of order.
Madam Speaker, who ever said that the Official Opposition never co-operates in helping process legislation in an easy fashion?

speakeroldname: Miss MacDonald (for Secretary of State of Canada) moved
speechtext: that the Bill be read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today with great pleasure to participate in the final stages of the debate of Bill C-93, the Canadian multiculturalism Bill. I want to tell you how proud I am to be the Minister of State for Multiculturalism during the final passage of this historic Bill.
This is a world-class Bill. It is a first of its kind. It is the solemn recognition by the Parliament of Canada on behalf of all Canadians of the fundamental importance of multiculturalism in our society. It gives concrete expression to the multicultural guarantee contained in Section 27 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. There are so many people I could thank for their work, foresight, and dedication in making this Bill possible, but I would like to single out two of them in particular: Mr. George Corn, immediate Past President of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council-
Hear, hear!
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext: -whose steadfast dedication for so many years has been an inspiration to so many, and David Crombie who, as Secretary of State, introduced the Bill on December 1 last-
A great guy; he was too good and that is why he left.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there have been discussions among the Parties. I think you would find consent for third reading to proceed immediately. I have discussed it with the other Parties, and I think that there may be Members who wish to address this matter beyond the hour of ten o'clock. We have agreed not to see the clock at 10 p.m.
We have also agreed that if a recorded division is demanded, such recorded division would be deferred until 3 p.m. tomorrow, and that there will be no quorum calls during that time. In the event that the proceedings should finish before 10 p.m., there would be no further business called by the Government and we would call it 10 p.m.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The House has heard the suggestions of the Hon. Minister of State. Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Saint-Denis on a point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext:
-and whose vision of being Canadian is a vision which encompasses us all.
I have followed the debate on Bill C-93 from its introduction to today. I have been impressed by the thoughtfulness of the many witnesses who came before the legislative committee. I have also been impressed by the thoughtfulness of the hundreds, yes, thousands of Canadians who have written both to me and to my predecessor. Underlying those submissions was the recognition that now was the time for the Canadian multiculturalism Bill.
Now is the the time for the Parliament of Canada to come together to recognize the multicultural reality of this nation and to celebrate our multicultural heritage.

Mr. Speaker, we have before us a Bill that provides an approach to multiculturalism based on co-operation, incentive, consensus and choice. We have before us a Bill that is a solemn recognition of what we are building together, all of us, in this great country of ours.


My appearance before the Legislative Committee at the beginning of April was one of my first official functions as Minister of State (Multiculturalism). On that occasion I indicated my intention of working with the Committee to improve and reinforce the Bill and make it more understandable to all Canadians. That is exactly what the Committee has done. It has reinforced the Bill, from the preamble down to the very last clause.

We were searching for the best way of expressing in this Bill our belief that multiculturalism is part and parcel of our Canadian identity and heritage. I feel that we settled on the best wording, that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of our heritage and our evolving identity.
We sought a way to make even stronger the system of parliamentary accountability which is at the heart of this Bill.
I think we found that way by the amendment that the Government of Canada and all its institutions shall undertake their responsibilities relative to the implementation of the multiculturalism policy of Canada. This one simple amendment gives concrete force to the commitment of the whole of the Government of Canada. We have not needed to resort to complex technicalities to deal with what was basically a very simple problem. As I have said, we will have in this Bill a very forceful parliamentary accountability process for the implementation of the multiculturalism policy of Canada. The combination of a Minister directly responsible to Parliament, clearer and more direct obligations for all Ministers and all federal institutions, a professional full-time departmental secretariat, a strengthened ministerial advisory committee, and a key scrutiny role for the standing committee make for a powerful, effective, yet co-operative approach to multiculturalism.
All across our nation Canadians are supporting Bill C-93. They see a Government that has listened and has worked to improve this Bill. They see a Government that is reaching out to all Canadians, offering everyone the vision of a new and stronger Canada. Just last week the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, whose members were all here today and may still be here, I hope, voiced enthusiastic support for this Bill and its speedy passage. They support this Bill because we worked cooperatively with them to strengthen it. This is what accountability to Parliament is all about. We have just proved that this Bill works. It works right now.
Some of my colleagues across the aisle still want some kind of formal commissioner with broad coercive powers. They seek to transplant an organizational model that suits one setting into new ground. What they have failed to recognize is the fundamentally different situation for the implementation of the multiculturalism policy in Canada in comparison with putting in force the Official Languages Act and carrying out the protection of fundamental human rights under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Canadian
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Human Rights Act, where the aim is to remedy breaches of legally established individual rights.

Mr. Speaker, the implementation of the multiculturalism policy will build upon many of the above-mentioned factors. Many of the problems Canadians face involve discrimination based on race, colour, and national or ethnic origin, and the Canadian Human Rights Commission has been mandated to meet those problems head-on. The Commitee amended the preamble to Bill C-93 to remind Canadians of the importance of the role of the Commission in the fight against discrimination.

This Bill encompasses a broad line of commitments, commitments which start in the preamble itself, which are expanded upon and given reality in the broad policy commitments contained in Clause 3(1) of the Bill, and which are made specific obligations for federal institutions in Clause 3(2). The Bill contains a very clear system of responsibilities and accountability for me as Minister and for every one of my ministerial colleagues. That accountability system is to the Parliament of Canada.
1 do not feel we need import into this very clear system an external compliance and monitoring agency. Such would be contrary to the very spirit of this Bill. This Bill is about the primacy of Parliament, and surely we in Parliament can monitor our own affairs. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we are serious about the very heart and specific commitments that we are making. That is why I was delighted to announce that we will be spending $192 million over the next five years to implement the new directions of the multiculturalism policy of Canada, an increase of $62 million in new funds for multiculturalism.
I have reoriented the programs of the multiculturalism sector to reflect the major themes of the Bill. Three areas are paramount:	race relations and cultural understanding;
heritage, cultures, and languages; and community support programs. That is also why I am establishing a multiculturalism secretariat to assist other federal Departments and agencies to implement the multiculturalism policy and to assist me in my important duty of reporting to Parliament on its implementation.
In our first Speech from the Throne delivered in the autumn of 1984 we identified certain key priorities. Two very important ones were, and remain, national reconciliation and social justice. This Bill before us today is about both these objectives. National reconciliation is all about being Canadian together. We can achieve our dreams. The Canadian multiculturalism Bill is part of this process.
This Bill is also about social justice. It stands as a landmark of a positive and pro-active approach to equality rights. We already have in the Charter, the Canadian Human Rights Act, and the employment equity legislation, a powerful set of anti-


Canadian Multiculturalism Act
discrimination instruments, but we need a pro-active policy approach by the Government on behalf of all Canadians to break down the barriers and misunderstandings that have sometimes kept us apart. That is provided in the Canadian multiculturalism Bill.
We pledge to ensure that federal boards and agencies reflect the multicultural reality of our society. We have kept that promise. In a little over three years we have doubled the number of ethnocultural appointments to important positions on boards, commissions, and agencies of the Government of Canada. We introduced the first numerical objectives for the Public Service for the hiring of visible minorities to strengthen and complement our existing programs for women, disabled persons, and aboriginal peoples. Our employment equity legislation and policies have taken our priority of social justice into the workplace.
Equality of participation is our objective throughout federal jurisdiction: the Public Service, federal contractors, and federally-regulated industries. This Government has been opened up to cultural and racial minorities as never before, and we shall continue to do so. That is fairness and it is a major step toward equality of opportunity, toward social justice, and toward national reconciliation, the things which were and remain key priorities.

Mr. Speaker, we are crossing the threshold of a new era within our federation. We are also entering into a new era in international relations. The years to come will reveal unprecedented perspectives of growth, prosperity and peace.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Multiculturalism Act is another symbol of that new era. It sets the tone. It recognizes our diverse origins, the fact that we and our ancestors come from the four corners of the earth, and it charts the course to be followed by all Canadians.

During the second reading debate on this Bill, the Hon. David Crombie quoted Dr. Barbara Ward, the noted British economist who has described Canada as the world's first international nation. I would like to take a moment to reflect on what that really means. It means that Canada is in essence a microcosm of the world. Other nations look to us for leadership in the areas of human rights and equality rights.
The passage of this Bill will send a signal to every corner of the globe that Canada truly is a land of equality and opportunity. We will show clearly that Canada is a land which respects and cherishes individual liberty and allows every person the freedom to cherish and maintain his or her own heritage.

Mr. Speaker, it is with confidence that I call on all Canadian men and women to support the ideals and the principles set
forth in the Canadian Multiculturalism Act. They reflect the cultural and racial diversity of our society; they show both where we have come from, and our course for the future.

This Bill is about co-operation and building together. It is about what makes Canada a very special nation. It is about our future.
The debate on this Bill is drawing to a close in the House of Commons, and I call on all Members from both sides of the aisle to join with me in affirming the principles of this Bill and in supporting this historic piece of legislation. I hope the Members of the other place will give this Bill speedy passage so that very soon the Canadian Multiculturalism Act will be law.
We are a nation of peoples from all corners of the globe. We believe in living together and working together as a family of individuals, and we are secure in our diversity. We are proud of our equality and we are confident in our future.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I also am very proud to speak on this Bill tonight because the principle expressed in this Bill is very important for our whole nation, for all the regions of our country and for all Canadian citizens who come from all over the world. It is a Bill which is very agreeable to many people throughout the country, but it is a Bill that this Parliament had the opportunity to improve, to strengthen by amendments, and thus to establish as a very sound piece of legislation which we can be proud of and which will guarantee multiculturalism a permanent future in this country.

I too am pleased to speak on third reading stage of Bill C-93, the Canadian multiculturalism Bill because the principle and the concept which underlie the multiculturalism Bill is one that I believe all Members from all sides of the House subscribe to and will defend and promote. However, the Bill could have and should have been made better.
This multiculturalism Bill was a window of opportunity that would have provided this Parliament, and particularly this Government, with the opportunity to listen to Members of the House of Commons, to members of the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism who tabled a unanimous report, and to the multitude of organizations which came before the Government and the committee to request and demand a number of things that would create the national fabric of multiculturalism in a piece of legislation.
While I agree with the principles and the concepts of the Bill, and while I certainly agree with some fundamental parts of it, I believe very sincerely and deeply that this Government to a certain degree missed an opportunity to try to deliver a piece of legislation that would have captured the imaginations


and furthered the aspirations of the current generation of Canadians and would have protected and embodied that enthusiastic support for future generations of Canadian citizens.
Bill C-93 is not a new initiative. It is not a unique undertaking. It had its roots and its beginnings in Bill C-84 which was introduced in the last Parliament and unfortunately died on the Order Paper after first reading because of the impending election. It was introduced by the then Liberal Minister, the Hon. David Collenette. It was not the entire answer. I admit and recognize that, and I have said so in debate in committee and in Parliament in the last number of years. Yet it was an important first step toward recognizing the need for an independent, comprehensive, strong and vibrant multicultural-ism Bill which would provide a legislative framework around policies and programs. It would provide that the policies and programs could not be here today and gone tomorrow with another Government. Somehow, they would become part of the legislative foundation upon which this country is built.
I believe the proof of that innovative idea of 1984 was that after the 1984 election, the Hon. Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta), the then Minister, sent Bill C-84 across Canada to various organizations and communities. He asked them for their input so that together we could build upon the strength of the 1984 legislation and try to correct the weaknesses.
It has been almost four years since this administration took office. This Bill provided the first opportunity we have had to discuss a major undertaking in multiculturalism policy. It has taken quite a while. It has taken almost the entire mandate of this Government to bring this Bill to fruition through a number of successive Ministers.
Beyond the speeches and rhetoric that come along with being an elected representative, beyond the speeches we hear from government Ministers who go across the land to various functions and picnics, I ask myself, as many other Canadians are asking themselves: "What other new directions have been taken in enhancing multiculturalism in the last four years?" What new initiative or expansion of existing programs was announced by the Government in 1984 when it assumed the national leadership of our country? I ask the Government how far the cause of multiculturalism has been advanced beyond what it found when it assumed office?
The answers to those questions go beyond the debate which has taken place over the last number of hours today and the second reading debate some months ago. Apart from that, however, I think there has been a vacuum in innovative and creative leadership on our multicultural policy that has been caused in part by the revolving door of Ministers we have seen in this portfolio during the four years of Conservative government. First, the Hon. Member for Lisgar assumed the portfolio, followed by the Hon. Member for Halton (Mr. Jelinek), then the former Member for Rosedale, and now the
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
current Minister from Montreal. That revolving door of Ministers has not engendered confidence among Canadians in this policy, or encouraged consistency. Each new Minister has different priorities which he or she wishes to pursue. That has not made for a very strong, consistent, or effective multiculturalism policy over the last four years.
I believe the successes of the Conservative Government in multiculturalism policies have been very few and far between. The Government has essentially tried to put its own brand on the directorate and failed. The Hon. Member for Lisgar had his difficulties. The Hon. Member for Halton wanted to introduce a "multiculturalism means business" policy and that did not fly.
Compare all that to previous Governments. Some people have asked why the Bill was not brought in earlier. That is a good question. Why was this not done earlier? Yet if we look at the record of previous Governments and the evolution of the various programs affecting multiculturalism, it speaks to a certain commitment and momentum that went beyond rhetoric.
For example, the first multiculturalism policy was enunciated in this House in 1971 by then Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau. In 1972 we saw the first Minister of State for Multiculturalism appointed. In 1973 was established the Consultative Council on Multiculturalism, the first advisory body to the federal Government on issues pertaining to multiculturalism. Then we had the cabinet decision to offer financial assistance to the performing and visual arts programs and projects. We had creation of the intercultural communications program, creation of the writing and publication program, and creation of the Canadian ethnic studies program.
In 1977 we saw the cultural enrichment program approved by Cabinet. In 1981 we had the first national conference on immigrant women, held in Saskatoon. There was the first national conference on heritage languages. The first national conference on multicultural heritage and education was held in Winnipeg. In 1981 we saw establishment of multicultural centres to allow individual ethnocultural communities to share resources and expertise and also help the voluntary sector organizations working in the area of cross-cultural communications.
In 1981 the Government included in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms Section 15 which prohibited discrimination because of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, or religion. Then of course there was Section 77 which ensured that the Charter would always recognize the multicultural heritage of Canadians. Also in 1981 we saw the national program to combat racism and a new race relations unit was established.
In 1982 Cabinet approved a doubling of the budget from $11.4 million to $25.4 million to allow for new initiatives and new programs in the social development area and to augment support for cultural retention. There was also the first national symposium on race relations and the law held in Vancouver. The first national conference on minorities and the media was


Canadian Multiculturalism Act
held in Toronto. There were guidelines issued on representative depiction of cultural diversity in the advertising of all government Departments, and funds provided for special training courses for visible minority Canadians in co-operation with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
In 1983 the then Minister responsible for multiculturalism introduced a notice of motion for the appointment of a special all-Party parliamentary task force on the participation of visible minority Canadians in Canadian society, to examine the situation of visible minorities and to look for constructive ways of improving race relations. That was approved by Parliament in June of 1983. Following that, we had the report Equality Now, tabled in March of 1984, and the Government response was tabled in June of that same year.
To go back to 1983, the Liberal Cabinet reaffirmed its commitment to cultural retention by tripling the funding and providing for inflationary increases for heritage language funding. New moneys allowed for the production of Canadian teaching materials as well.
Then we had the establishment of the national resource centre for heritage language at the Ontario Institute for Studies in Education. There was the announcement of a strategy for inclusion of visible minority Canadians in the affirmative action programs of the Public Service, by the then President of the Treasury Board.
In 1984 there was new emphasis on making all sectors of Canadian society more aware of the multicultural reality which is Canada. There was a national conference focusing on business, communications, and culture. Encouraged by the then Minister, the Canadian Advertising Advisory Board established an informal referral service to advise members on the use of visible minorities in the general field and profession of advertising. New moneys were allocated and funds spent for visible minorities in a disadvantaged position as a result of institutional discrimination and racial biases. Then of course, as I mentioned, there was introduction of the multiculturalism Bill, as well as Criminal Code amendments to strengthen legislation against dissemination of hate propaganda in Canada.
Also in 1984, in co-operation with chiefs of police, there was the first national symposium on policing in a multicultural, multiracial society, held in Vancouver. The Cabinet at that time committed a further $5 million endowment to serve as a continuing and dynamic memorial to the courage and perseverance of the nisei generation of the Japanese-Canadian community, and to support initiatives developed by concerned Canadians to combat systematic racism in our society.
That, briefly and not all encompassing, is an example of what I meant by the evolution and building up of multiculturalism policy by previous Governments. I believe that exercise of establishing a foundation and building upon it has not occurred in the last four years of the current Government, until this piece of legislation was brought forward. Why?
Before the last election it was very clear that the then Opposition had very ambitious programs, projects, promises, and dreams for multiculturalism policy.
In fact, on June 2 at a major conference in Toronto, the then Opposition Leader, today's Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and the first Minister responsible for multiculturalism under the 1984 administration, made 46 different promises in the field of multiculturalism. They talked about cultural retention, the maintenance of liaison between government officials and the directorate, a review, increased funding, and new programs. As I look at the list of promises made, I ask myself how many of these promises were acted upon.
At that particular conference the Hon. Member for Lisgar committed that if he were to become the Minister the budget of the multiculturalism directorate would be doubled. As we debated the Estimates in 1985, 1986, and 1987 we saw that the budgets were, in some cases, lower than in previous years.
The lack of follow-up on promises cannot be better depicted than by the Japanese Canadian redress issue. The then Leader of the Opposition, the present Prime Minister, on the last day of the previous administration in Question Period, criticized the then Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau, for not having gone far enough on the issue of Japanese Canadian redress. The then Opposition Leader made it a national issue, not only by raising it in the national forum but by committing himself, his Party, and his government-to-be to a process of negotiation, apology, and compensation which went beyond what the Government of 1984 was prepared to deliver. He made that a campaign issue and raised it at various campaign stops.
For four years since then the promise has been continuously avoided and ignored. At no time, for instance, did the Prime Minister meet with the National Association of Japanese Canadians despite calls, letters, and urgings from Ministers and members of the Opposition to indicate that he would have been able to offer some mobilization, some encouragement to break the log-jam which has existed for the last four years.
The first Minister of multiculturalism, the Hon. Member for Lisgar, promised negotiations when he came into office and then backed away preferring to hide behind discussions. The Hon. Member for Halton was Minister of State for Multiculturalism at the time. When he addressed this issue it seemed to me that he was more interested in trying to divide that community and in moving away from the commitment made to negotiate with the National Association of Japanese Canadians. Rather than doing that, there were questions about whether the NAJC was the dutifully elected body to speak on behalf of the Japanese Canadian community.
We then had the former Member of Parliament for Rose-dale who brought an informal and gutsy approach to his service in this Parliament. I have a great deal of respect for him. In his capacity as Mayor of the City of Toronto he


captured, to a certain degree, the imagination of his generation in the sixties and seventies. Ele brought that refreshing attitude to this Parliament. However, when all the dust had settled on the issue of Japanese Canadian redress, the matter was not moved ahead. It was stagnating in a corner of Canada's Parliament. The current Minister is the fourth Minister to initiate discussions on Japanese Canadian redress.
I am not suggesting that the previous administration was pure on this issue. I disagreed with the previous administration's conclusion about redressing the past. I have tried, in my capacity as a Member and as the critic on multiculturalism for the Liberal Party, to overcome that position. I have tried to send the message that political Parties are able to change, are able to recognize that the policies of a previous time are not meeting the needs and aspirations of the current citizenry and leadership within the Japanese Canadian community. We were prepared to move.
However, the real issue is with the current administration. The previous administration, rightly or wrongly, took a position and defended it. This administration, led by the Prime Minister, took one position before the election and a different position for four years running. There is a question in terms of the acknowledgement, apology, and compensation, and then there is the process. The substance was never given an opportunity to materialize because there was no legitimate process allowed for that substance to be agreed upon.
I tell the Prime Minister, as rumours about an impending election circulate around the country and certainly around this Chamber, that it would do honour, not only to this Government but to this Parliament, to try to put behind us a very sad and sorry chapter in Canadian history, to try to recognize that injustice and to enable the 10,000 to 12,000 Canadians of Japanese ancestry who survive from that time to see the day when the pain in their bodies and souls will, to a certain degree, be eradicated.
I suggest that the process must be given a chance in order for a solution to be reached. The Minister and the National Association of Japanese Canadians must meet and set out the parameters. That must be followed up by negotiations with officials from both parties. Those officials must then go back to their respective organizations and analyse what happened during the bargaining session. The Minister and the national association must then come back together and try to resolve the differences which may still exist.
If there are still differences at that time, the Prime Minister should be involved in order to try to overcome the hurdles and the gulf between the NAJC and the Conservative Minister of multiculturalism. If that is not satisfactory we should consider a third party, be it a committee of this House or a one or two-person commission.
I understand the frustration with yet further study, further commissions, and further committees. However, we need to resolve this issue. It is simply too important to allow it to languish on the Order Paper, in the corridors, and in the
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
endless meetings which have taken place on this issue. This is one issue which must be resolved. It points to the lack of leadership and commitment which has symbolized the multicultural policy of the Government.
Another aspect which deals with resolve and commitment is that of funding for the Department of Multiculturalism. Within a conference back in June, 1984, the Government of the day was saying that immediately upon assuming office it would double the budget of the multiculturalism directorate as did the Liberal Government in the mid-1980s. It was the smallest directorate of any federal Department, with an expenditure of $24 million or $1 per year per person on a per capita basis.
In this year's Estimates we were debating expenditures of a Department that had less moneys granted it this year in the Estimates than in 1985 or 1986. Not only did the Government fail to keep up with the cost of inflation, it failed to keep up with real money from previous years. In the last three to four years communities have pleaded with the Government and expressed their concerns. Members of the Opposition and government members on the standing committee have urged the Government for more funding.
Suddenly, with rumours of an impending election, the Minister has decided to increase the budget. That increase does not necessarily take place this year, but it is a commitment by Parliament for the next five years. Suddenly the Government will increase the funding.
Some may ask why we are complaining if this answers our concerns and the community and the Department are promised more money by the Government. Our complaint is that the budget of this Department continues to be hooked to the rollercoaster cart of an election. For some years the Department's budgets were smaller than those of the previous years. We argued against this in the House and in committee as well as throughout the country. It is quite a coincidence that suddenly the budget is increased right before a general election. The fact that this increase is a commitment by Parliament for five further years is unsatisfactory. I do not know of many other Departments that receive their financial backing in such a manner.
We have argued for a continuing, secure and encompassing set of financial resources to build the infrastructure of a Department that will not have to languish for four years with a budget that increases during election time and comes down the roller-coaster on the other side of the election. That does nothing for program delivery, for efficiency, or for the confidence Canadians will have in a Department that is well run and well managed.
The same can be said for the recent announcement increasing the advertising budgets for the third language media. The third language media plays a significant and increasing role in trying to bring the works of the federal Government and


Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Parliament closer to the readers of their newspapers and to the audiences of multilingual and multicultural radio and television programming. They have been complaining for a number of years about cut-backs by the Government in terms of advertising and that the money has been going primarily to English and French media. They have been complaining that there should be advertisement from all federal government Departments rather than simply the federal multiculturalism Department. The Government has ignored these complaints for three and a half years. Suddenly, again by coincidence, a few weeks ago at a major conference in Toronto the money was found to increase third language media advertising.
I am not arguing against further increases. I am not arguing that those important media outlets should not receive Government support like other newspapers and radio and television stations. I am asking that we try to stop delivering funding to the multicultural portfolio in that fashion, to get away from the short-term frills to buy favour with various constituencies at election time, and to replace it with a more long-term, genuine and comprehensive budget that will probably do more, even if the funds are smaller, than those promised during an impending election.
Not only would we have a program and a Department that could build upon its success, it would go a long way in removing the emotional cynicism that exists in certain quarters of this country about the role of a federal multiculturalism policy. One cannot put a price on the kind of educational direction that would attempt to convert those who may be suspicious of the value and advantage of such a policy.
That confidence was not engendered by the actions of some members of the Canadian Multiculturalism Council, an advisory group of individuals who give of their time and their energies to try to promote and enhance a multiculturalism policy. For the most part, they do a very credible and proud job.
However, that confidence was not instilled when, on February 24, 1986, the Deputy Chairman of the Canadian Multiculturalism Council, Mr. Peter McCreath, wrote a confidential memorandum to the then Minister of State for Multiculturalism, the present Minister of Supply and Services. He basically admitted from his own perception that the Canadian Multiculturalism Council was nothing more than an outreach of the Conservative Government. Clearly, that is not its role.
He stated on page 2 of his memorandum that there were three strains of commonality among the members of the Canadian Multiculturalism Council: "One of them is that they are all committed supporters of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, the Government of the Right Hon. Brian Mulroney and the Minister of State for Multiculturalism".
He went on to say: "Our voluntary commitment to the Government and our wish to see it survive beyond the next general election together gives us the luxury of being able to assess the situation and present our recommendations solely in
the context of what we truly believe is in the best interest of Canada and of the Conservative Government of the day".
As if that were not enough, he said: "Whatever weaknesses may be inherent in any recommendation to government from the CMC, they at least reflect and form advice and opinion from a selection of the Government's principal supporters across Canada".
That advisory committee to the Government of Canada is there to mobilize that assistance and advice, to percolate those ideas and aspirations from the grass root community organizations and various cultural constituencies across the country. That kind of manipulation, promotion and position by that advisory council is an abuse. That is not the purpose of the CMC. It is not there to protect and support, at any cost and at any interest, the particular political expediencies of one particular Party. The Canadian Multiculturalism Council exists to advise the Government on the best policy of multiculturalism. Yet, when individuals like the Deputy Vice-Chairman articulates very clearly, not once, twice, but three times, in the body of his memo that he considers the CMC as principal supporters of the Conservative Party there is something wrong.
There is something even more wrong when the Minister of the day, the former Member of Parliament for Rosedale, refused to remove that individual, not so the individual would not be able to serve the Government or the country or his interests in the area of multiculturalism, which I am sure he has done, but to send a message to Canadians that the Minister and the Government disavow themselves from the views of this individual. That was not done despite repeated urgings in Parliament, in committee, and in personal correspondence. That is the deep hurt. One would have thought there would have been the political courage to stand up and say: "No, that is not what the CMC stands for".
In September, 1986 some people suggested that that perhaps was an inadvertent slip by one Member and that it was water under the bridge, but we received a document from the Metro Toronto caucus of the Conservative Party. Outlined in a secret memorandum to the Minister was a number of different topics including immigration, internal communication, media, multiculturalism, appointments, prime ministerial and ministerial scheduling. It is a memorandum that is shocking in terms of the recommendations. Under immigration, for instance, the memorandum talks about trying to take advantage of ministerial permits. It states that Canada issued approximately 6,500 ministerial permits in 1985. Of these, only some 10 per cent were issued by the Minister's office. The balance was used by visa officers, CIC, and departmental staff. It states the political potential of ministerial permits is obviously being allowed to fall by the wayside. What this memorandum is saying in between the lines is: "Let us Conservative Members suggest who the ministerial permits should go to in order to help us win some friends".


The memorandum goes on to say that the perception of Tories sidling up to communities in the ethnic areas and opening the floodgates at our borders, as it were, can severely damage enthusiasm for the Party at the traditional grass roots level and thereby nullify any gains in the newer communities. It states that a watchful eye must be kept on the creeping hostility to immigrants which, especially in times of economic duress, is nearly fully dormant and represents a political back lash if acceptable selection standards are not maintained. The Conservative approach to immigration, therefore, must successfully combine intelligence with understanding and selectivity with compassion. Firm but fair was the slogan that was recommended.
The memorandum goes on to talk in terms of the media. It states the long-standing neglect by Tories of the third language press must be reversed before the next general election. That is exactly what happened only a few weeks ago. Good relations with third language media must be achieved if breakthroughs in Metropolitan Toronto's ethnic ridings are to be expected. Ministers, Members, the PMO, and the Party should all contribute to the current political effort aimed at ethnocultural communities and respond to the need to develop a detailed strategy on the federal level pertaining to the ethnic media.
The memorandum goes on to state that the value of the third language media in communicating government policy is generally not recognized. Advertising budgets do not allow for the publicizing of ethnic appointments. MTV suffers from a lack of advertising support from the Government, and given the station's plans to develop into a network, the problem of bad revenue causes considerable political damage.
The memorandum goes on to talk about multiculturalism. The Conservative caucus in Metro Toronto states in the opening paragraph that the committee believes that the articulation of a distinctive Conservative policy on multiculturalism is overdue and as such an urgent priority. Ethnocultural communities must be made to understand precisely why they should give their ballots to the Government rather than to the opposition Parties.
In terms of funding, what I find to be very offensive is the paragraph where the memorandum states that trends in funding of various ethnocultural groups were the next topic examined by the committee. It was stressed that there should be nothing arbitrary about funding cuts or increases. "Liberal funding patterns", whatever that means, "should be disposed of and a politically intelligent PC pattern should take their place. This may be accomplished by a gradual process of funding cuts and reallocations". Some grants managed there are properly reflective of ridings and the ethnic element within them. There was a strong feeling that leadership on grants should come from the caucus and from committees. "Members of Parliament who have access to grant cheques to present at ethnic functions should endeavour to take advantage of such opportunities". The memorandum goes on and on in terms of the very offensive approach and attitude taken in this report toward multiculturalism, appointments, and the role of the
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Prime Minister in trying to target a number of various ethnic communities that I could read into the record but will not.
I believe it goes to show this Member of Parliament the type of mind-set that exists above and beyond perhaps the general rhetoric that we hear in terms of a multiculturalism Bill.
The former Minister of State for Multiculturalism, the Member of Parliament for Rosedale, initiated the multiculturalism Bill last year, after work was done by the previous two Ministers under this Conservative administration. That Minister was actually opposed in concept to a multiculturalism Bill. Despite the introduction of a Liberal multiculturalism Bill in 1984, despite the commitment of the Members of Parliament for Lisgar and Halton, the former Member of Parliament for Rosedale was against the concept because he preferred-and I suppose the Government preferred it- instead of operating under a Multiculturalism Bill to make amendments to the Citizenship Act under the guise of multiculturalism. They thought that would be good enough.
I believe the former Member of Parliament for Rosedale essentially moved on a multiculturalism Bill only after he discovered that the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism was in fact studying and making a report upon which the major recommendation would be a comprehensive and significant multiculturalism Bill. At that time the Minister shifted his commitment. The committee and various organizations such as the Canadian Ethnocultural Council and others who supported the committee's ideas and visions were really responsible for moving the Government into building from that 1984 Bill and trying to crystallize this piece of legislation in Canada's books.
As I mentioned, the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism, which was representative of all three political Parties, provided a very detailed examination into the whole area of multiculturalism. In the end, it gave the political green light to this Government and to this Minister to proceed on a very comprehensive Bill that would encompass and embody the type of aspirations existing in the country among various member communities. That committee report was not an attempt simply to put on paper a few ideas or to try to stitch together a number of recommendations. It was the product of a very long and detailed process. It was a report that was established after the committee held 16 public meetings and heard from a variety of witnesses, including verbal testimony and briefs from such groups as the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, as well as responses from 20 different federal Departments, about where they thought multiculturalism should go in terms of their respective Departments.
Another major source of input was from the written briefs that the former Minister, the Hon. Member for Lisgar, requested and received from various organizations. These briefs were obtained and distilled as information pertinent to the area of study and reference.


Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Extensive information on multiculturalism and related policies was also obtained from the multiculturalism sector. A further major source of information was the consultative meeting on race relations hosted by the multiculturalism sector in August of 1986, and other documents. Then, of course, there were the various meetings of the committee in camera to try to digest all this information into a coherent direction.
The committee on the multiculturalism policy, a separate minister for multiculturalism, as well as a separate official multiculturalism commissioner would report to Parliament. There were recommendations built on those three general areas which ran deep in terms of the feelings that communities had and in terms of the goals and objectives that organizations brought to the committee. We made a number of recommendations, 18 in all, ranging from provincial and municipal policies to a separate line Department, to a multiculturalism commissioner, to an Act respecting multiculturalism, and so on.
